en: In that he gathers [the materials] from here and there,
that is the reason for the "gathering" (sambhāra) of the gathering-rites;
from wherever a part of the fire has been deposited, from each of those places he gathers it, and thus he truly causes him to prosper through glory alone.
He prepares it with animals as it were, with a pair as it were.
Then he scrapes it;
whatever of this earth has been stepped upon or trampled, that very thing he [removes] from it.
He digs this out; thus he establishes it upon the very earth that is fit for sacrifice. Therefore, he scrapes [the ground].
Then he sprinkles it with water.
This, indeed, is the collection of water: that he sprinkles it with water. Now, as for the water—

The waters indeed provide food, for the waters are food; therefore, when the waters come to this world, then food is produced here. Thus, by means of that very food, he causes him to prosper. The waters, indeed, are women.
By means of the pair, the bull and the fire, he thus causes him to prosper through procreation.
Indeed, all this is pervaded by water; having thus obtained him by means of water, he establishes him. Therefore, he gathers water. Then he gathers gold.
Agni, indeed, meditated upon the waters, thinking, "May I become united with them in sexual union.
He united with them and poured his seed into them; that became gold. Therefore, it resembles fire, for it is the seed of Agni.
Therefore, they find it in the waters, for he poured it into the waters. For this reason, one does not wash it, nor does one do anything [to it].
Now, he makes it glorious, for that [gold] is indeed the seed of the gods; verily, by means of glory he thus endows him with glory.
He establishes Agni as one who possesses seed and is complete; therefore, he gathers gold.
Then he gathers salt.

Yonder sky indeed bestowed these cattle upon this earth; therefore they say that saline soil is "cattle-rich," for these are truly cattle. Thus, he directly causes him to prosper by means of cattle themselves, which have come from yonder to this earth.
They consider the essence of these two, heaven and earth, to be established in them;
he thus provides this [sacrificer] with the essence of these very two, heaven and earth. Therefore, he gathers the *ūṣas*.
Then he gathers the dung of a mouse.
Mice indeed know the sap of this earth;

therefore, moving deeper and deeper into this earth, they are fattest, for they know its sap. Wherever they know the sap of this earth, from there they cast it up; thus he endows him with the very sap of this earth.
Therefore, he collects mole-droppings; for they say of one who attains prosperity, "He is full of *purīṣa*.
Now, *purīṣa* and *karīṣa* are the same thing; thus it is for the sake of securing this very thing that he collects mole-droppings.
Then he collects pebbles.
The gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another.
This earth was quivering like a lotus leaf; the wind used to blow it about, and it went now to the gods and now to the asuras. Wherever it went to the gods— 2.1.1 [9]
Then they said: "Come, let us make this foundation firm; upon it, being fixed and unshakable, let us establish the two fires.
From that, we shall exclude our rivals from this [earth].
Just as one would stretch a hide with pegs.
In this way they consolidated this foundation; thus this foundation became firm and unshakable.
Upon that firm and unshakable foundation, they established the two fires. Thereupon, his rivals were excluded from it. 2.1.1 [11]
In the same way,
he now strengthens this foundation with pebbles; upon that firm and unshakable foundation he establishes the two fires, and thereby he excludes his rivals from it— therefore there are pebbles.
He collects these five materials. The sacrifice is fivefold; the animal is fivefold; there are five seasons in the year.

Regarding this they say: "There are only six seasons of the year. [They reply: "In that case, the procreative union is performed deficiently; for from a deficiency these creatures are born, and that which is deficient is more excellent. Therefore, there are five. But if it is said that there are indeed six seasons of the year, then Agni himself is the sixth of them; thus, in this way, it becomes non-deficient. 2.1.1 [14]

Regarding this they say: "One should not gather even a single requisite. For all these requisites exist upon this earth; when one establishes the fires upon this earth, he thereby obtains all the requisites. Therefore, they say, "One should not gather even a single requisite.
Nevertheless, one should indeed gather them, for it is precisely when one establishes the fires upon this earth that [the requisites are obtained].

He obtains all those requisites; whatever is accomplished by means of the requisites when they have been gathered, that indeed comes to pass. Therefore, one should certainly gather them. One should establish the two fires under the Kṛttikās.
The Kṛttikās are indeed Agni’s lunar mansion; it is consistent with nature for one who establishes the sacred fires under Agni’s lunar mansion.
Therefore, one should establish the fires under the Kṛttikās.
One, two, three.
Or rather, there are four other constellations, but these, the Kṛttikās, are the most numerous;
thus he attains abundance. Therefore, one should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās.
Indeed, these do not deviate from the eastern quarter.

Indeed, all other lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) deviate from the eastern quarter; therefore, these two [fires] of his come to be established in that very eastern quarter. For this reason, one should establish [the fires] under the Kṛttikās. Now, as to why one should not establish [the fires] under the Kṛttikās:

In the beginning, these were indeed the wives of the Ṛkṣas; for they used to call the Seven Seers "the Ṛkṣas. They became deprived of their union, for the Seven Seers rise in the north while these [stars] are in the east. Indeed, he who is deprived of his union suffers as it were; therefore, one should think, "Lest I be deprived of my union."
Therefore, one should not offer the oblation under the Kṛttikās; yet, indeed, one may offer it. For Agni is the mate of these [stars], and by means of Agni as their mate—
Therefore, one should establish the fires on a day when [the moon is] full. One should establish the two fires under the asterism Rohiṇī.
Indeed, it was under Rohiṇī that Prajāpati, desiring offspring, established the two fires; he [thereby] produced offspring.

He created those creatures; once created, they stood fixed in a single form, like red cows (rohiṇī). That indeed is the reason for the name "red cow" (rohiṇī) of the Rohiṇī constellation. He who, knowing this, establishes his sacred fires under Rohiṇī, truly becomes abundant in offspring and cattle. Indeed, under Rohiṇī, cattle [thrive].
"Let us kindle the two fires so that we may attain our desire among men"—thus they said, and they attained the desire among men.
That very desire which cattle attained among men, that same desire he attains among cattle who, knowing this, establishes the fires under the Rohiṇī constellation. 2.1.2. [8]
One should establish the sacred fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa.
For Mṛgaśīrṣa is indeed the head of Prajāpati; the head is prosperity, for the head is indeed prosperity.
Therefore, of whatever region a person is the most excellent, they say of him: "He is the head of that region. [It brings] prosperity.
He who, knowing thus, establishes the sacred fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa, truly goes [to the world of heaven].

Now, as to why one should not establish the fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa: this body of Prajāpati is indeed that [constellation] where they [place him]. 2.1.2. [9] Now, as to why one should not establish the fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa... where they [place him].

They say that he pierced it with that three-jointed arrow; he abandoned this body, for the body is indeed unfit for sacrifice and devoid of power. Therefore, one should not establish the sacred fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa.
Or rather, one may indeed establish them.

"Indeed, there is no dwelling-place, no sacrificial portion, and no body belonging to this god that does not belong to Prajāpati; therefore, one should indeed establish [the fires]. One should perform the re-establishment of the fires under the Punarvasus. 2.1.2. [11] One should establish the two fires under the Phalgunīs.
These Phalgunīs are indeed Indra’s lunar mansion;
they are also his namesakes, for Indra’s secret name is truly Arjuna, and these stars are called Arjunīs.
They are referred to cryptically as "Phalgunīs," for who is worthy of uttering Indra’s secret name? It is Indra.

The sacrificer is indeed Indra; thus he establishes the two fires under his own constellation. Since Indra is the deity of the sacrifice, by this means his establishment of the fires becomes possessed of Indra. He should establish them under the first two [nakṣatras]; for then the will (*kratu*) is directed toward him from the front. Or he may establish them under the latter two; for then what is better than tomorrow (*śvaḥśreyasa*) comes to him as something subsequent. 2.1.2. [12]
One who desires, "May it be given to me," should place the fires in his hand; for that which is given by the hand is indeed given directly, and so it is surely given to him. 2.1.2. [13]
One should establish the sacred fires under the constellation Citrā.
Once upon a time, both the gods and the Asuras, being offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another;
they both desired to ascend to yonder world, the very sky. Thereupon, the Asuras piled up the fire-altar called Rauhiṇa.
"By this we shall ascend to that world.
2.1.2.[14] Indra indeed reflected: "If they build this [altar], they will surely overcome us from that very place. He...
A man calling himself a Brāhmaṇa came along, having tied up a single brick.
He said, "Come now, let me also lay down this one. They said, "So be it," and he laid it down.
Consequently, their fire-altar remained uncompleted after only a very short time.
Then he said, "I will surely give her back to whom she belongs. Having approached her, he pulled her out.
When she had been pulled out, Agni went out; following Agni’s going out, the Asuras went out. He [pulled her] out... those... her.
Having made the *eṣṭhakās* into thunderbolts, he cut off their necks.
Then the gods, having come together, said: "We have indeed become wonderful (*citra*), since we have slain so many enemies. That, indeed...

The Citrā [constellation] possesses the quality of being variegated; it indeed becomes variegated. He who, knowing this, establishes his sacred fires under Citrā, slays his rivals and slays his hateful enemy. Therefore, this constellation is to be sought after by a kṣatriya alone, for he, as it were, desires to strike down his rivals and strives to conquer them. 2.1.2. [18]
In the beginning, indeed, these were various ruling powers (*kṣatra*).
Just as that sun is [now], so did he, upon rising, take away their vigor and ruling power; therefore he is named Āditya, because he took away (*ādatta*) their vigor and ruling power. 2.1.2 [19]

Those gods said, "Whatever those powers (kṣatrāṇi) were, they truly were not powers. That indeed is the reason for the "star-ness" (nakṣatra-tva) of the stars. Therefore, one should have the sun as one's star, for he is their vigor.
He takes up the *kṣatra*. Now, if he should desire a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), this sun is indeed the faultless lunar mansion.
By means of this very auspicious day, he may obtain whatever among those lunar mansions he might desire; therefore, it should be under the sun as his lunar mansion. 2.1.3.1.
Spring, summer, and the rainy season—these seasons are the gods;
autumn, winter, and the cool season—these are the fathers. That half-month which waxes is the gods; that which wanes is the fathers. Day indeed is the gods; night is the fathers.
Furthermore, the forenoon belongs to the gods and the afternoon to the ancestors.
These seasons, indeed, are both the gods and the ancestors. Whoever, knowing this, invokes them as "the gods and the ancestors," for him [they come].

The gods go to the invocation of the gods, and the ancestors go to the invocation of the ancestors; the gods favor him at the invocation of the gods, and the ancestors favor him at the invocation of the ancestors, who, knowing this, invokes them saying, "O gods, O ancestors! 2.1.3.
[3] When he turns northward...
When he turns toward the north among the gods, he then belongs to the gods and protects the gods;
but when he turns toward the south, he then belongs to the fathers and protects the fathers. 2.1.3 [4] As for where he turns toward the north...
In that case, one should establish the two fires; the gods are free from evil, and he strikes away evil.

The gods are immortal, and there is no hope for immortality for him who establishes them at such a time—he merely attains a full lifespan. Now, when the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is turned toward the south, he who establishes the fires at that time [does so for the ancestors]: the ancestors are not free from evil, and he does not strike away evil; the ancestors are mortal.
He who establishes [the fires] when his life is still far from its end, he indeed establishes them.
Spring is Brahman;
summer is Kṣatra; the rainy season is Viś. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa [should establish them] in spring.
For spring is indeed the *brahman*; therefore, a Kṣatriya should establish the sacred fires in summer, for summer is indeed the *kṣatra*.
Therefore, a Vaiśya should establish them in the rainy season, for the rainy season is indeed the *viś*. 2.1.3.
[6] Now, he who might desire:
"May I be endowed with spiritual luster," thinking thus, he should establish the fires in spring; for spring is indeed the Brahman, and he certainly becomes endowed with spiritual luster.
2.1.3. [7] Now, as for one who might desire:
"He who desires, 'May I be a kṣatriya in prosperity and fame,' should establish the sacred fires in summer;
for summer is indeed the kṣatriya, and he truly becomes a kṣatriya in prosperity and fame.
2.1.3. [8] Now, as for him who should desire—

"May I be rich in offspring and cattle," [thinking thus], he should establish the fires during the rainy season. The rainy season is indeed the common people (*viś*), and the common people are food. He who, knowing this, establishes the fires during the rainy season, truly becomes rich in offspring and cattle. These, then, are the seasons. 2.1.3.
[9] They are indeed these seasons.

Both [classes of people] have their evil struck away; the sun indeed strikes away their evil as it rises, striking away the evil of both these classes. Therefore, whenever the sacrifice should come upon him, he should then establish the two fires; he should not wait for tomorrow. For who knows what tomorrow will bring for a mortal? 2.1.4.1.
On the day before his *agnyādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires) is to take place, he should eat only during the daytime.
For the gods indeed perceive the mind of a human being; they know that his *agnyādheya* is to be on the morrow, and all the gods come to his house. They...

They fast in his houses; that is the Upavasatha. Now, it is indeed improper for one to eat before others among men have eaten, so how much more so for one to eat before the gods have eaten? Therefore, one should eat only during the day, though even then it may be at will.

One should eat at night, for there is no performance of vows for one who has not established the sacred fires; for as long as he has not established the fires, he remains merely a human being. Therefore, even in that case, he may indeed eat at night if he so desires. Regarding this, some tie up a goat.
"The goat belongs to Agni; it is for the sake of Agni’s all-pervasiveness," so they say. But one should not do that.
If he has a goat, he should give it to the Āgnīdhra priest in the morning; by that very act, he obtains that desire.
Therefore, one should not pay heed to that [argument]. 2.1.4. [4]
Then they cook rice for four persons to eat, thinking,

"By this we shall gratify the meters. They say, "Just as one would tell a driver who is about to set out on a journey to ensure his vehicle is well-provisioned, so it is with this," but that is not the case.
Or rather, whatever the Brāhmaṇas—both those who are officiating priests and those who are not—who dwell in his family do, by that alone he attains that desire;
therefore, one should not pay heed to that [other ritual].
Having made a cavity for pouring clarified butter into it...

Having poured clarified butter [onto the fire], they place three *aśvattha* fuel-sticks upon it, having anointed them with ghee, while reciting verses containing the words "fuel" (*samidh*) and "ghee" (*ghṛta*), saying, "We have obtained this essence of the *śamī* tree. He who places them on the fire for a full year beforehand would indeed obtain that desire; therefore—
One should not pay heed to that.
Regarding this, Bhāllaveya said:
"Just as when someone is about to do something else..."
"He would act as if he were saying one thing while intending to say another; he would proceed by one path while intending to go by another.

Thus, for those who would cook this *cātuṣprāśya* rice-mess, it would be a failure indeed; for that is not appropriate, in which fire one should place a fuel-stick with a Ṛg-verse, a Sāman-chant, or a Yajus-formula."

He should either place [the fire] upon it or offer an oblation into it; for they may take away that [fire] as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or cause it to go out, thinking, "They are taking this [fire] as a sacrificial fee, and the Anvāhāryapacana fire will remain. Thus they cause it to go out. 2.1.4.
Now, the gods are awake.
Thus he turns toward the gods; being more divine, more wearied, and more ascetic, he establishes the two fires.

Even so, he may sleep at his pleasure, for there is no performance of vows for one who has not yet established the fires, since as long as one has not established the fires, he remains merely a human being; therefore, he may indeed sleep at his pleasure. 2.1.4. [8]
Regarding this, some, having churned [the fire] before sunrise,
lift it up toward the east after sunrise, saying, "We thus encompass both day and night for the fulfillment of the out-breath and the in-breath, and of mind and speech. But one should not do so.

He should indeed perform both; thus they become established for him before sunrise. For, having churned [the fire] before sunrise, they draw it out toward the east at sunrise. Now, if one were to churn the Āhavanīya fire after sunrise, he would surely complete that rite. The gods are indeed the day.
The ancestors have not shaken off evil; mortals do not shake off evil.
He who churns before sunrise dies before his full span of life. The gods have shaken off evil; he shakes off evil. The gods are immortal;
there is no hope for immortality [for him], yet he reaches a full lifespan. The gods are prosperity; he goes to prosperity. The gods are glory; he indeed attains glory.
He who, knowing thus, churns the fire after it has risen, becomes such.

2.1.4. [10] Regarding this they say: "Since the fire is not established with a Ṛc, nor with a Sāman, nor with a Yajus, by what then is it established? It is indeed by the Brahman that this fire is established. Speech is the Brahman; of that speech, truth alone is the Brahman. Now, these [are the following]:

The *vyāhṛtis* are indeed truth; therefore, by means of truth alone is this [sacrifice] performed. "Bhūḥ"—with this Prajāpati generated this [earth]; "Bhuvaḥ"—[he generated] the intermediate space; "Svaḥ"—[he generated] the sky. So much indeed [is the world]. 2.1.4. [11]
All this, as far as these worlds extend, is sustained by all of it.
"Bhūḥ"—Prajāpati indeed generated the *brahman* [priesthood] with this; "Bhuvaḥ"—the *kṣatra* [nobility] with this; "Svaḥ"—the *viś* [common people] with this. This much, indeed, is all this.
Everything, as far as the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya, is supported by everything. 2.1.4.
[13] By means of *bhūḥ*, Prajāpati indeed generated himself;
by *bhuvaḥ*, he generated offspring; and by *svaḥ*, he generated cattle. This much, indeed, is this world.
"Everything as far as the self, offspring, and cattle—by means of all this, the fire is established.
2.1.4. [14] He indeed says, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ.
By this much alone he establishes the Gārhapatya fire; then...
If one were to take up all [the formulas], with which would he take up the Āhavanīya fire? He leaves two syllables remaining;
thereby these [formulas] do not become exhausted. With all five of them, including "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he takes up the Āhavanīya fire.
These amount to eight syllables. The Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the metre of Agni.
He establishes him by means of this very *candas*. 2.1.4.
[15] When the gods were about to establish the two fires, the Asuras and Rakṣases guarded them, thinking, "The fire shall not be born; neither of the two fires shall arise."
"You shall establish [it]," they said. Because they protected it, therefore they are called *rakṣāṃsi*.
Then the gods beheld this thunderbolt: the horse; they raised it up in front, in a place free from fear and free from destruction.
Fire was born in a windless place; therefore, where one is about to churn fire, one should say, "Bring a horse.
It stands to the east; thus one raises the thunderbolt. In its safety and security, free from destruction, fire is born in a windless place.
2.1.4. [17] That [horse] should indeed face the east.

For his vigor increases immeasurably: even if he should not find a draft-ox, any horse whatsoever will do; and if he should not find a horse, there must at least be an ox, for this indeed is the kinship of the ox. 2.1.4 [18]
Where they carry him facing eastward,
they lead the horse in front; thus, striking away the destructive spirits and demons from the front, they carry him forward in safety and freedom from harm.
They should indeed carry him away in that very same manner, so that he (the fire) may attend upon him facing westward. For this Agni is the sacrifice;
thus the sacrifice enters him facing westward, and the sacrifice quickly approaches him. But as for why [he should not do so] facing away...

The sacrifice indeed turns away from him; and if someone were to say of him at that moment, "The sacrifice has turned away from him," it might well come to pass exactly so. This, moreover, is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
They would surely carry him off in exactly the same way as this [breath] would treat him if it were turned away from him;
for the breath enters him only when it is turned toward him, but since it becomes turned away from him, the breath indeed becomes turned away from him.
If someone were to say of him in that situation, "The breath has turned away from him," it is possible that it would indeed be so. 2.1.4. [21]
This sacrifice is indeed he who blows here.
They should carry him in such a way that this [wind] attends to him from the front; for thus the sacrifice enters him from the front, and the sacrifice quickly approaches him. Then...

Because he turns away, the sacrifice indeed turns away from him. If someone were to say to him then, "The sacrifice has turned away from you," it is possible that it would indeed be so. This, moreover, is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
They would surely carry him away in exactly that way, as if he were treating him face-to-face;
for the breath enters him from the front, and because it turns away from him, the breath indeed turns away from him.
If someone were to say of him in that situation, "The breath has turned away from him," it is possible that it would indeed be so; therefore—
In that very same manner they should carry [the horse]. 2.1.4.
[23] Then he makes the horse step upon [the fire-altar]; having made it step upon it, he leads it eastward; he then turns it back again.
He releases it upwards, thinking, "May this vigor not be turned away from him";
therefore he brings it back again. He places it upon the footprint of the horse.
Vigor is the horse; verily, he thus bestows vigor upon him. Therefore, he places it on the footprint of the horse.
He first touches it silently.
Then he raises it up, then he touches water; with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he places it down for the third time.
These worlds are indeed three; thus he attains these very worlds—this is one [way].
Now, this is the second.
He touches [the fire] at the front silently; then he lifts it up with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! and places it down with the second [verse].
For whoever lifts a burden while not being established upon this [earth], he is unable to lift it and it crushes him. 2.1.4. [27]

When he touches [the water] silently, that is for him to find support in this [earth]; thus supported on this earth, he establishes the fire-altar, and thereby he does not waver. Now, Āsuri Pāñci and Mādhuki Sarva indeed maintained this very point as follows: "Everything."
Or, as if it were not yet finished, he may lift and place it with the first [formula] alone, namely "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ";
that indeed is the unfinished [rite]. Therefore, he may do whichever he desires.
Then, having gone around by the front—
Having taken hold of the front half of the firebrands, he recites:

"Like the sky in abundance, like the earth in width. By saying "like the sky in abundance," he means "just as that sky is vast with stars, so may I become great"; and by saying "like the earth in width," he means "just as this [earth is wide]."

"O Earth, vast one, may I become thus broad"—this is what he says by this. "On your back, O Earth, place of divine sacrifice"—for he places him on her back. "The fire-eating Agni, for the sake of food, I place"—Agni is indeed a food-eater; "may I become a food-eater," this is what he says by this. This is indeed a prayer; if he should so desire, he should mutter this, but if not...
One might desire [the fruit], yet one should not pay heed to it.
Then he worships with the verses of the Queen of Serpents: "This spotted bull has stepped forth; he has settled before his mother."
"Going toward his father, he moves within the luminous realms; breathing out from his breath, the Great One has looked out upon heaven;
he shines through thirty stations; speech is bestowed upon the bird at every dawn throughout the days.
Thus, whatever of this [sacrifice] remains unobtained here—whether by means of the ritual materials, the constellations, the seasons, or the placing of the fire—that is thereby obtained.

By this, everything of his becomes attained; therefore, he worships with the verses of the Serpent Queen (Sarparājñī). Regarding this, they say: "One should not worship with the verses of the Serpent Queen. This earth, indeed, is the Serpent Queen;
whatever one establishes upon her, thereby one attains all desires. Therefore, they say: "One should not worship with the verses of the Serpent Queen."

Having drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, he offers the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti). Now, as to why he offers the full-offering: when he produces this Agni for himself, he produces him as an eater of food; therefore, he provides this food for him, just as one would for a young child.
Just as one would cover the breast for a newborn calf, so does he cover this food for him.
Being appeased by this food, he desists from the subsequent oblations being cooked; for indeed, [if he were not appeased, he would consume them]. 2.2.1. [2]
It would burn either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer, for these two move closest to it if one were not to offer this oblation into it; therefore, one offers this oblation. One offers it full.
Everything is indeed full; with everything he thus satiates him. He offers with the utterance *svāhā*;
the utterance *svāhā* is indeed undefined, and everything is undefined; with everything he thus satiates him. That which Prajāpati [created]... 2.2.1. [4]... indeed.

He offered the first oblation with the words "Svāhā!"—that is indeed how he offered it; this [oblation] is its underlying cause (nidāna), therefore one offers with "Svāhā! In that [oblation], he gives a boon; the boon is indeed everything, and thus he satisfies him with everything. 2.2.1. [5]

Regarding this they say: "Having offered this very oblation, one need not pay heed to the subsequent sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*); by this alone one attains that desire for which one prepares the subsequent offerings.
He, indeed, prepares [the offering] for Agni Pavamāna.

The purifying breath (pavamāna) is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa); he thus bestows the vital breath upon this [sacrificer]. He bestows it upon him by means of the *vetu* formula, for the vital breath is food, and this oblation is food. 2.2.1. [7]
Then he offers to Agni Pāvaka.
Food indeed is Pāvaka; thus he places food in him.
He places it in him by means of this very [offering], for this oblation is food manifestly. 2.2.1. [8]
Then he offers to Agni Śuci.
Vigor, indeed, is pure; for that which shines forth from him is his pure vigor. He thus bestows vigor upon him. He bestows it upon him by means of the *vetasa* reed, when—
Verily, he offers this oblation for him, and then his vital power blazes forth pure.
Therefore they say:
"Having offered this very oblation, one need not pay further heed to the subsequent offerings; by this alone one [attains that]."
"He obtains whatever desire he desires because he offers the subsequent oblations"—therefore, one should indeed offer the subsequent oblations.
For that which is "yonder" (adaḥ) is, as it were, invisible; it is as if one says, "this is that. Now, when he offers to Agni Pavamāna...
The purifying wind (pavamāna) is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa). When one is born, then there is the vital breath;
and as long as one is not yet born, one breathes along with the vital breath of the mother. Or rather, it is just as when [the breath] has been born:
he thereby bestows this vital breath upon him. 2.2.1 [11]
Now, as for why he offers to Agni Pāvaka:
food indeed is purifying (pāvaka); thus, at the very moment he is born, he bestows this food upon him. 2.2.1 [12]
Now, as to why he offers to Agni Śuci:
vigor indeed is pure; for when one grows by means of food, then one attains vigor. Having thus caused him to grow by means of food, he then bestows this pure vigor upon him.
Therefore, [the offering is] for Agni Śuci (the Pure).
This very same reality, however, appears as if inverted.
For it was when Agni turned away from the gods toward human beings that this occurred.
He reflected: "Let me not be entirely enveloped by men. He then distributed these three bodies of his among these worlds:
that form of his which was *pavamāna*, he placed in this [earth].

Then he deposited that which was purifying upon the earth, that which was bright in the intermediate space, and that which was pure in the sky. The seers who existed at that time perceived this: "Agni has indeed turned away from us with his entire self.
Therefore, they offered these oblations for him. 2.2.1 [15]
When he offers to Agni Pavamāna,
by that he obtains whatever form of his is on this earth; then, when he offers to Agni Pāvaka, [he obtains] whatever form of his is in the intermediate space.

By this [offering], he thereby obtains that very form of his; then, when he offers to Agni Śuci, he thereby obtains that form of his which is in heaven. Thus, indeed, he establishes the entire Agni without omitting anything. Therefore, one should certainly offer the subsequent oblations. 2.2.1. [16]
The first oblation has its sacrificial grass (*barhis*) separate;
the two subsequent ones have their grass in common.
This world is indeed the first oblation, this intermediate space is the second, and the sky is the third. For this [earth] is indeed broad.
"The earth trembles as it were, the atmosphere trembles as it were, and yonder sky—even both of these would rise up against her.
Therefore, they have the same sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
All the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) consist of eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*).
The Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the metre of Agni; he thus establishes him by means of his own metre. All those [verses] amount to twenty-four potsherds;
the Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the metre of Agni; he thus establishes him by means of his own metre. 2.2.1. [18]
Then he offers a pap (caru) to Aditi.
For he who offers these oblations indeed departs from this world; for he goes as if ascending these worlds. 2.2.1 [19]
When he offers a pap to Aditi—Aditi is indeed this earth, and she is the foundation;
thus he establishes himself upon this very foundation. That is why he offers a pap to Aditi. 2.2.1 [20]
Regarding this, they say: "The two Virāj verses should be the *saṃyājyās* for it;
for this [earth] is a Virāj. Or, "Two Triṣṭubh verses;
for this [earth] is a Triṣṭubh. Or, "Two Jagatī verses; for this [earth] is a Jagatī. Yet, they should indeed be two Virāj verses. 2.2.1 [21]

A cow is its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). For this earth, like a cow, milks all desires for human beings; a cow is a mother, and this earth, like a mother, supports human beings. Therefore, a cow is the sacrificial fee. This is one way of proceeding. 2.2.1 [22]
Now follows this second [offering]:
he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni alone. For that which is for Agni Pavamāna, for Agni Pāvaka, and for Agni Śuci is, as it were, indirect.
Thus, as it were, he establishes him directly and openly; therefore, after [the offering] for Agni, he prepares a *caru* oblation for Aditi.
Whatever is the significance of the *caru*, that is its significance.
They indeed slay this sacrifice.
When they stretch this [sacrificial cord], and when they press the King (Soma), they kill him;
when they quiet the animal and dissect it, they kill it; with the mortar and pestle, and with the lower and upper grinding stones, they kill the Haviryajña. 2.2.2. [2]
This very sacrifice, being struck down, was not capable of functioning. The gods made it capable by means of sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).

Because they made it capable (*adakṣayan*) by means of sacrificial gifts, they are called *dakṣiṇā*. Therefore, whatever part of the sacrifice falters when it has been struck down, [it is restored by them].

It is by means of these sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) that he thus makes this [sacrifice] successful; then the sacrifice becomes truly prosperous. Therefore, he gives sacrificial gifts. He should indeed give six of them.
There are six seasons in a year; the year is the sacrifice, [and] Prajāpati.
To whatever extent the sacrifice is, to whatever its measure is, with so many [cows] he bestows it.
Twelve he should give. 2.2.2. [4]
There are indeed twelve months in a year; the year is the sacrifice, Prajāpati.
As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is, with so many [gifts] he causes it to prosper.
He should give twenty-four.

There are indeed twenty-four half-months in a year; the year is the sacrifice, Prajāpati. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is, with so many [cows] he makes it successful. This is the measure of sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
However, one should give more according to one's faith. Now, as to why he gives sacrificial gifts: 2.2.2 [6]
Truly, there are two kinds of gods:
the gods who are gods, and those Brahmins who have heard the sacred texts and are learned in them—they are the human gods.
For them, the sacrifice is divided into two parts: the oblations belong to the gods, while the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belong to the human gods.

Of human gods—that is, of Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred tradition—he gratifies the gods with oblations and the human gods, the Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred tradition, with sacrificial gifts. Both these classes of gods, being pleased, place him in the world of bliss. 2.2.2 [7]
Just as one would place seed in a womb, even so do the officiating priests place the sacrificer in the world.
When he gives this to them, it is because they have brought him safely to this state; such is the nature of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās). 2.2.2. [8]

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Both of them were indeed without self, for they were mortal; indeed, being mortal, they were without self. Among those mortals, Agni alone was immortal. Him—

Both [gods and asuras] lived upon the immortal [Amṛta]. Whenever they killed one of them, he would indeed become that very thing again. Then the gods remained as it were the smallest in number; they wandered about performing austerities and practicing rituals, thinking, "May we overcome our rivals, the asuras, who are subject to death. They [discovered] this immortal [element], the establishment of the sacred fires (Agnnyādheya).
They saw it. They said: "Come, let us place this immortality within ourselves;
having placed this immortality within ourselves, we shall become immortal and indestructible."
"We shall overcome our mortal rivals by means of the *staryān*," they said.
They replied, "This Agni belongs to both of us; let us rather announce it to the Asuras. They said, "We shall indeed establish the fires; what then will you do?"

They said, "Then we shall simply bury him here; burn grass here, burn wood here, cook rice here, and cook meat here. Because the Asuras buried him there, humans eat by means of that very thing. 2.2.2 [14]

Then the gods placed him within their own selves; having placed this immortality within their own selves, they became immortal, they became invincible, and having become invincible, they overcame their mortal enemies. And so does he [who knows this].

He places this immortality within his inner self; there is no hope for immortality [for one who does not do so]. He attains a full lifespan and becomes invincible; indeed, no rival, even one seeking to strike him down, can strike him.
Therefore, when one who has established the sacred fires and one who has not established them compete, the one who has established the fires prevails, for he is truly invincible.
He then becomes immortal. 2.2.2.[15] Now, when they churn him here, he breathes forth as soon as he is born; for he is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
By means of the fire, he thus causes him—who already exists as born—to be born; he breathes out again, and thereby places him within his own self.
Thus, this fire becomes established within his very self. Having kindled it, he fans it into flame.
"I shall sacrifice here; here I shall perform good deeds"—with these very thoughts he kindles him, that fire which is established within his inner self.
"He has come between; he has separated himself," so it is said.

Indeed, no one at all can pass between him and this [fire] as long as he lives, for this fire has been established within his inner self; therefore, one should not care if it goes out, for this fire which has been established within his inner self does not go out as long as he lives. 2.2.2. [18]
These fires are indeed the vital breaths:
the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya are the Prāṇa and the Udāna, and the Anvāhāryapacana is the Vyāna. 2.2.2 [19]

Now, for this very establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), truth alone is the ritual service (*upacāra*). He who speaks the truth—just as if one were to sprinkle a kindled fire with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), so does he cause it to blaze up; for him, [the fire] becomes greater and greater still.

His splendor increases day by day, and he becomes better day after day. But as for him who speaks untruth—just as if one were to sprinkle a kindled fire with water, so does it extinguish him; his splendor becomes less and less day by day, and he becomes worse day after day. Therefore, one should speak only the truth. 2.2.2 [20]

Now, his kinsmen said to Aruṇa Aupaveśi, "You have indeed grown old; kindle the sacred fires. He replied, "Do not say that to me. Remain restrained in speech; one who has established the sacred fires must never speak untruth, nor should he ever speak while speaking [untruth]."
"One should not speak untruth; truth alone is the proper conduct. Varuṇa, desiring sovereignty, undertook this [vow];
he attained sovereignty. Therefore, whether one speaks it or not, it is Varuṇa.

They say, "He is a king. Soma was desirous of glory; he became glory. Therefore, both he who obtains [the fruit] in the Soma sacrifice and he who does not come together to behold this very glory; indeed, he becomes glorious and attains sovereignty, who, knowing thus, establishes the fires. 2.2.3 [22]

In the fire, indeed, the gods deposited all forms— both those that are domestic and those that are wild— either when they were about to set out for victory, or for the sake of moving at will, or thinking, "May this one, the best protector, guard us. 2.2.3 [23]

Agni desired to hide those [limbs]. Having gathered them together, he entered the seasons, thinking, "I shall return. When Agni had thus disappeared from them, the gods were distressed, saying, "What is to be done here? What wisdom is there here? 2.2.3 [24]
Then Tvaṣṭṛ perceived this re-establishment of the fires;
he established them and thereby attained the beloved abode of Agni.
He then cast off from himself both kinds of forms: those that are domestic and those that are wild.

Therefore they say, "Forms indeed belong to Tvaṣṭṛ," for every form belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ; yet other creatures stand as far as he [Tvaṣṭṛ] does, and as he is. For what purpose, then, should one perform the re-establishment of the fires?
In this very way, he approaches the beloved abode of Agni;

he bestows upon him both kinds of forms, those that are domestic and those that are wild, and these two kinds of forms are seen in him. That is indeed the highest state; they long for him, and thus he prospers; it is also for the sake of the world. 2.2.3 [26]
This sacrifice belongs to Agni;

Agni is light, the burner of evil. He burns away his evil, and he becomes light itself here through prosperity and fame, and light there in the world of merit. This, then, is why one should establish the fires. 2.2.3 [27]
One should indeed install it during the rains.

The rains are all the seasons, for the rains are indeed all the seasons; therefore, people look back upon the years, saying, "In those days we had rain, in those days we had rain. And yet, it is truly the rains.
Indeed, the form of all the seasons is present in the rainy season. When they say, "It is as if summer," that too occurs in the rainy season;
and when they say, "It is as if winter," that too occurs in the rainy season. Thus, the rainy season begins with the rainy season.
Now, this very thing is its indirect (parokṣa) form.
That which blows from the east is the form of spring;

that which thunders is the form of summer; that which rains is the form of the rainy season; that which lightens is the form of autumn; and that which holds back the rain after it has fallen is the form of winter.
The rainy season is all the seasons. He entered the seasons; verily, he now fashions him from the seasons. 2.2.3. [29]
The sun alone is indeed all the seasons: when it rises, it is spring; when it is the time for milking (saṃgava), it is summer;
when it is midday, it is the rainy season; when it is afternoon, it is autumn; and when it sets, it is winter.
Therefore, one should establish the sacred fires at midday during the winter season; for then this [sun] is nearest to this world, and thus he fashions him from that which is nearest to the middle.
Indeed, this person is as if made of shadow.
That evil which clings to him becomes his smallest part here;
it is cast down as if beneath his feet. Thus he strikes down that evil with the smallest part.
Therefore, one should indeed install the fires at midday. 2.2.3 [31]
He indeed draws it out with *darbha* grasses.

Previously, he draws it out with wooden sticks; if he were to use wooden sticks first and then [darbhas], he would create a state of kinship and cause conflict. *Darbha* grasses are water, and rain is water.
He enters the seasons with water; verily, he fashions him from water. Therefore, he draws it out with *darbha* grass.
With two leaves of the *arka* tree, having made a cake of rice, at the place where he is about to establish the *gārhapatya* fire—
He places it there; he establishes the *gārhapatya* fire.
Having made a barley cake on two *arka*-palāśa leaves, he places it where he is about to establish the *āhavanīya* fire;
he establishes the *āhavanīya* fire there. By means of these two former fires, he thus interposes them.
Saying this, they would not do so; for by means of the nights alone, the two [the sun and the moon] become hidden.
2.2.3. [34] He offers a sacrificial cake on five potsherds dedicated to Agni.
For it, there are five-footed *paṅkti* verses.

There are offering-verses (*yājyā*) and invitatory-verses (*anuvākyā*). There are five seasons; he entered the seasons. It is from the seasons that he thus fashions him. 2.2.3. [35] The entire [sacrifice] belongs to Agni.
For in this way Tvaṣṭṛ approached the beloved abode of Agni; therefore, the entire [sacrifice] belongs to Agni.
It is so; therefore, they proceed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
For when one wishes to perform a rite exclusive to oneself (*niṣkevalya*) for a kinsman or a friend, he does so as if in secret.

One sacrifice is indeed shared by all the gods (*vaiśvadeva*), while this other one is exclusively for Agni (*niṣkevalya*). Since that which is as if hidden is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), therefore they proceed in a low voice.
He performs the final after-offering (*anuyāja*) loudly.
"For he then becomes as one who has performed his duty, for everyone indeed understands what has been done.
Having caused the announcement to be made, he says: 2.2.3.[38] He says, having caused the announcement to be made.

"Recite the offering prayer for the fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*)," he says; that is the indirect form belonging to Agni. But he should rather say, "Recite the offering prayer for the fires (*agnīn*)," for that is the direct form belonging to Agni.
He performs the sacrifice: "May the fires partake of the clarified butter, *vauṣaṭ*; may Agni partake of the clarified butter, *vauṣaṭ*; may [the fires] through Agni partake of the clarified butter."
"May the fire of the *vaṣaṭ*-call enjoy the clarified butter; *vauṣaṭ*! [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.3.40].
Then he says, "Svāhā to Agni!"—if it is the *ājyabhāga* for Agni, [he says], "Svāhā to Agni Pavamāna."

"May they be held for Pavamāna, svāhā! To Agni Indumat, svāhā!"—if [the oblations] are to be held for Agni Indumat; "To Agni, svāhā! May Agni, pleased by the clarified butter, enjoy the clarified butter"—with these words he performs the sacrifice. Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni."

He recites the *ājyabhāga* for Agni: "Awaken Agni with a hymn, as he is being kindled, the immortal one; may he place our offerings among the gods. For when he has been removed from the fire, he is, as it were, asleep;
by this [verse], he truly awakens him and rouses him. He performs the sacrifice with: "May Agni, enjoying it, partake of the clarified butter. 2.2.3. [42]
Now, if they should be intended for Agni Pavamāna, he should say, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Pavamāna! He then recites:
"O Agni, you purify our lifespans; bring us strength and nourishment; drive far away the malevolent."
For thus it becomes an offering to Agni; Pavamāna is indeed Soma, so they lead [the sacrifice] away from the *saumya* butter-portion, and he offers with the formula:
"May Agni Pavamāna, being pleased, partake of the butter. 2.2.3. [43] Now, if the fires should be maintained for Agni Indumat.

"Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Indumat," he should say; he then recites: "Come here, O Agni, let me speak these other songs to you; grow strong by these drops. Thus indeed he becomes connected with Agni. Soma, indeed, is the *indu*; therefore they lead him away from the *ājyabhāga* belonging to Soma with the words: "May Agni, accompanied by *indu*, enjoy the clarified butter."
"Let him know," he says; thus he sacrifices and in this way makes everything belong to Agni.
Then he says, "Recite for Agni" regarding the oblation;
"Sacrifice to Agni"; "Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"; [sacrifice to] Agni.
"Offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice!"—when he says this, he is effectively saying, "Sacrifice to the gods," or "Sacrifice to the fires.

He sacrifices: "May Agni accept [the portion] for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure; *vauṣaṭ*! May Agni accept [the portion] for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure; *vauṣaṭ*! The divine Agni *Sviṣṭakṛt*... Thus, the third [offering] belongs to Agni himself, and in this way, the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) belong to Agni.
He performs them. Indeed, these are the six case-endings: he offers four in the *prayāja*s and two in the *anuyāja*s. There are six seasons;
he entered the seasons, and it is from the seasons that he now fashions him.
There are either twelve or thirteen syllables;
for there are either twelve or thirteen months in the year. He entered the seasons from the year; thus, he fashions him from the seasons and from the year. Not even two [syllables] more.

One should not commit a kinship offense against that which is born together; for even if two things should be together, [the thought] "let them go apart" or "let it partake" is indeed the form of the *prayāja* offerings, while "for the winning of wealth, for the bestowing of wealth" is the form of the *anuyāja* offerings.
His sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is gold.

This sacrifice indeed belongs to Agni; gold is the seed of Agni, therefore gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Or rather, it is an ox, for he is connected to Agni by his carrying-power; for his carrying-power is as if burnt by fire, since "Agni is the carrier of the oblation for the gods. He indeed carries [the sacrifice].
Therefore, among humans, the ox is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 2.2.4.
Prajāpati alone indeed existed here in the beginning. He thought, "How indeed might I be reproduced? He exerted himself. He...

He performed austerity; he brought forth Agni from his mouth. Because he brought him forth from his mouth, therefore Agni is an eater of food (*annāda*). He who knows this Agni to be an eater of food becomes indeed an eater of food. Now, it was at the very beginning that he brought him forth among the gods.

Therefore, Agni—this which is called "Agni"—is indeed so named. As soon as he was born, he went forward; for he who goes first (*pūrva*) goes at the front (*agra*). Thus they call him "Agni," and that is his nature as Agni. Then Prajāpati reflected.

"He has indeed produced this eater of food for himself, namely Agni; for there is no other food here besides me, or else he would not eat it. At that time, the earth was indeed made bare, for neither herbs nor trees existed; that alone was his concern. 2.2.4 [4]
Then Agni turned toward him with his mouth wide open.
As he was terrified, his own greatness departed from him; for speech is indeed his own greatness, and it departed from him. He sought an oblation within his own self, and he wiped [it] away.
Because he wiped it off, this [part] is hairless and this [part] is hairless; there he perceived it to be either an oblation of ghee or an oblation of milk, yet in truth, both were indeed milk.
It did not, however, satisfy him.
"O mixed one, laugh away that evil!"—from this [utterance] the plants (*oṣadhayaḥ*) came into being; therefore they are called "plants. He wiped his hand a second time;
there he discovered another oblation, either an oblation of ghee or an oblation of milk—but indeed, both of these are simply milk. 2.2.4. [6]
She pleased him.
He hesitated, wondering, "Should I offer the oblation? Or should I not? His own greatness (Svaḥ) spoke to him, saying, "Offer it!
Then Prajāpati understood: "It is my own greatness that has spoken to me. Thus he [offered].

He offered with "Svāhā! Therefore, it is offered with "Svāhā! From that, he who shines yonder arose; from that, this one who blows came into being; and from that very source, Agni turned away. Having offered, Prajāpati [proceeded].
Prajāpati was born from the consuming fire; he saved himself from death. He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, is born with that same progeny with which Prajāpati was born.
Thus indeed does he save himself from the consuming fire, from death. 2.2.4. [8]
Wherever he dies,
wherever they place him upon the fire, there he is born again from that very fire;
then the fire burns his body alone, and just as one might be born from a father or a mother, even so is he born from the fire.
Indeed, he who does not offer the Agnihotra is never truly born; therefore, the Agnihotra must be offered. This very thing is the origin of doubt—that Prajāpati doubted.
He who was wavering took his stand upon what is better; he was born from that which was being consumed, and he saved himself from Agni, from death.
He who thus knows this birth of doubt—whatever he doubts, he indeed takes his stand upon what is better.
Having offered the oblation, he wiped [the vessel].

From that, the *vikaṅkata* tree came into being; therefore, it is the tree fit for sacrifice and fit for sacrificial vessels. From that, these heroes of the gods were born: Agni, he who blows here (Vāyu), and Sūrya.
Truly, he who knows these heroes of the gods, a hero is born to him. 2.2.4 [11]
They said, "We indeed belong to our father Prajāpati; come, let us create that which shall belong to us. Having enclosed themselves, they praised with the Gāyatra [Sāman], without the Hiṅkāra.
That which they enclosed became the ocean; this earth itself was the sacrificial enclosure (stava).
Having offered praise, the gods stepped forward, thinking, "Let us return. Then the Earth, having become a cow, looked up at them.

The gods perceived the *hiṃkāra* of the Sāman; they realized, "This is the *hiṃkāra* of the Sāman. Prior to that, the Sāman was indeed without a *hiṃkāra*. This very thing is the *hiṃkāra* of the Sāman in the cow. Therefore, this [cow] is a source of livelihood; for he who knows this *hiṃkāra* of the Sāman in the cow becomes, indeed, a source of livelihood. 2.2.4. [13]

They said, "Truly, we have brought forth something auspicious, we who have brought forth the cow; for this [cow] is indeed the sacrifice, for without the cow no sacrifice is performed; she is indeed food, for whatever food there is, that is the cow.
This, indeed, is their name.
This is the sacrifice; therefore, one should set it aside, saying, "It is good, it is meritorious. Indeed, many such [names] belong to him;
the sacrifice becomes inclined toward him who, knowing this, sets it aside, saying, "It is good, it is meritorious. 2.2.4. [15]
Agni set his mind upon her, thinking, "May I be united with her. He united with her and poured his seed into her;
that became milk. Therefore, when a cow is pregnant, this [milk] is cooked, for it is Agni's seed. Therefore, if...
If it is on the dark [fortnight], when it is Rohiṇī, it becomes bright like fire; for fire is the seed of Agni, therefore what is first milked is hot, for fire is the seed of Agni. 2.2.4.
[16] They said: "Come, let us offer this! To whom shall we offer this first?"

"It is for me," Agni said; "It is for me," he who blows here [Vāyu] said; "It is for me," Sūrya said. They could not reach an agreement. Having failed to agree, they said, "Let us go to our father Prajāpati. Whichever of us he declares as the first to whom this [oblation] should be offered, to him we shall offer it first. Thus they went.
They said to their father Prajāpati, "To whom will they offer this first?

He said, "To Agni; Agni shall produce his own seed by means of Anuṣṭhā, and thus you shall be reproduced. And [it shall be offered] to you—[namely] to Sūrya—and whatever of the oblation he consumes, that belongs to him who is this [wind]."

"Blows forth"—for even now they offer this to them in exactly the same way: to Agni in the evening and to Sūrya in the morning. And whatever of the oblation he consumes, that very thing belongs to him who blows here. Having offered these, the gods—
They procreated this progeny which is their progeny; they won this victory which is their victory. Agni won this very world, Vāyu the intermediate space, and Sūrya the sky.
He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, procreates that very same progeny which these [gods] procreated.

From this they were born; they conquered that victory which they won by this. Indeed, he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, becomes a sharer in the same world as these [gods]. Therefore, the Agnihotra must indeed be offered. The sun, verily, is the Agnihotra.

Because it rose from the top of this oblation, therefore the sun is the *agnihotra*. When he offers in the evening after [the sun] has set, [he thinks], "While this [sun] is present here, may I offer"; and when [he offers] in the morning before [the sun] has risen...
"He offers [the oblation], thinking: 'While this [sun] exists here, I shall offer into it. Therefore, they say that the sun is the Agnihotra.
Then, when it sets, having become an embryo, it enters into the fire as its very womb; that embryo—"
All these creatures follow after you; for they lie down within the womb, sleeping in harmony.
Now, when it is night, he makes this hidden, for embryos are, as it were, hidden.
When he offers in the evening after the sun has set—
He offers this oblation while it is still an embryo; he performs this rite while it is still an embryo.
Because he offers the oblation while it is still an embryo, therefore these embryos live without eating. 2.3.1 [5]

Now, as to why he offers in the morning before the sun has risen: he thereby causes him (the sun) to be born; thus, having become brilliance, he rises shining forth. Indeed, he would never rise if he were not to offer this oblation into him; therefore, indeed, [he offers].
He offers this oblation.
Just as a snake might free itself from its skin,
so he frees himself from the evil of the night, just as a snake [frees itself] from its skin.
Thus he is released from all evil; indeed, he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, is released.
Following the procreation of this very [Agni], all these creatures are procreated; for they are emitted according to their purpose. 2.3.1 [7] Now, he who [offers] before the setting of the sun...
He draws out the Āhavanīya fire. These rays are indeed the Viśve Devas;

and that which is the supreme light is either Prajāpati or Indra. Now, the Viśve Devas come to the house of one who offers the Agnihotra. From him whose [fire] they find not yet drawn out, the gods depart. That [light], indeed, belongs to him.

That fails because the gods depart from it; they say that its failure belongs both to him who knows [this] and to him who does not, for he has gone to his rest before being lifted up. 2.3.1. [8] Now, as for one who [goes to rest] before the setting of the sun:
He draws out the Āhavanīya fire;
just as one would wait upon a superior who is about to arrive with a prepared dwelling, so it is in that case.
When they come to him whose fire has been drawn out, they enter his Āhavanīya and settle within his Āhavanīya. 2.3.1 [9]

When he offers in the evening after the sun has set, he offers to these [gods] who have entered into Agni; and when he offers in the morning before the sun has risen, he offers to these very ones while they have not yet departed. Therefore, for those who offer after sunrise...
"We consider the *agnihotra* to have been interrupted," so indeed said Āsuri; "just as one might enter an empty dwelling, so it is with that.
2.3.1. [10] Indeed, this living is twofold.
Both that which has roots and that which is rootless—both these, O gods, men subsist upon. Animals are rooted; plants have roots.
Having eaten the plants that have roots and having drunk water, from that this essence arises. 2.3.1 [11]

When he offers at evening after the sun has set, he thinks, "I shall offer this essence, this life-force, to the gods, that we may live upon what belongs to them here. And when he eats thereafter during the night, he eats only the remains of the offering, having already set aside his portion.

For by offering the Agnihotra with the remains of the oblation, one becomes an eater [of food]. 2.3.1.[12] Now, when he offers it in the morning before sunrise, he thinks: "I shall offer this essence, this life-force, to the gods; for this [essence] belongs to them."

"We live upon him. Therefore, when he eats from that [offering] during the day, he eats only the remnants of what has been offered (*hutocchiṣṭa*), having set aside no sacrificial portions (*niravatta-bali*).
For indeed, one who offers the *agnihotra* is an eater of the remnants of what has been offered.
Regarding this, they say: "Other sacrifices come to a conclusion, but the *agnihotra* alone does not conclude. 2.3.1 [13]

The twelve-year period is indeed finite; however, this very [practice] is infinite. For, having offered in the evening, he knows, "I shall offer in the morning," and having offered in the morning, he knows, "I shall offer again in the evening. This is the Agnihotra that is never-ending; following its endlessness, these creatures are endless.

They are born; indeed, one who knows this Agnihotra as "not standing near" (anupasthita) is not abandoned by prosperity and is born with offspring. Having milked it, he places it on the fire. 2.3.1 [14]
"It is uncooked when it is raw," they say; "therefore, one should offer it when it is cooked.
But one should not make it overcooked. For if one were to make it overcooked, he would burn it; and seed that is burnt is indeed incapable of procreation.
Therefore, one should not make it overcooked. 2.3.1 [15]
One should offer the oblation immediately after placing it on the fire.
For this very semen of Agni is indeed cooked by that [act]; and because they place it on the fire, it is thereby indeed cooked.
Therefore, one should offer the oblation immediately after placing it on the fire. 2.3.1.[16]
He illumines it with that [fire], thinking, "Now it is cooked. Then he pours water back into it for the sake of pacification and for the sake of the completeness of the essence;
for when it rains here, then plants are born, and having eaten the plants and drunk the water, from that [the milk arises].

This sap arises from that; therefore, for the sake of the completeness of the sap, if there should be only milk for him to drink, he should say, "Sprinkle a little [of it] on top," for the sake of the completeness of the sap and indeed for the sake of its finality. 2.3.1. [17]
Then he draws up four [portions of milk];

for this milk is prepared in four ways. Then, taking a fuel-stick, he runs forward for the sake of the *samiddha* offering. Without having set down the previous oblation, he offers it; for if he were to set it down, it would be as if—

For if he were to set it down before bringing food for someone, it would be as if he had brought food for that person and then merely set it down; but by setting it down after having brought it near, he makes these two—mind and speech—which are these two oblations, possess distinct powers. Mind and speech, indeed, are these two oblations; thus he unites both mind and speech.

Therefore, he turns back this mind and speech; though they are the same, they are as if not the same. 2.3.1.[18] He indeed offers twice in the fire, wipes [the vessel] twice, eats twice, and draws up four times; that makes ten.
The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is indeed the Virāj; thus he brings this sacrifice into correspondence with the Virāj.
When he offers into the fire, he offers among the gods, and therefore the gods exist; then, when he wipes [the vessel], he offers among men.
He offers it to the fathers and to the plants; therefore the fathers exist and the plants exist. Then, when he has offered and eats, he offers it to human beings; therefore human beings exist.
2.3.1 [20] Those creatures indeed that are not included in the sacrifice—

Those who have been defeated are indeed thus; likewise, those offspring here that have not been defeated, he causes them to participate in the mouth of the sacrifice. Therefore, cattle are made participants along with humans, since cattle follow after humans.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said:
"One should certainly not think of this as being like a formal sacrifice (yajña); rather, it is like a domestic sacrifice (pākayajña).
For whatever one cuts off with the sacrificial ladle (sruk) in another sacrifice, all of that one offers into the fire; but in this case, [it is offered] directly into the fire."
Having offered and stepped back, he sips water and licks [the vessel]; for this is like a *pākayajña* sacrifice, and that is its animal-like form, for the *pākayajña* is indeed animal-like.
This is the one oblation at the beginning.

That very oblation which Prajāpati offered, then these [beings] took their stand as it were in the form of cattle—namely Agni, he who blows here (Vāyu), and Sūrya; therefore this second oblation is offered.
2.3.1. [23] As for that first oblation:

She is the deity of the Agnihotra; therefore, one offers to her. Now, that which is the subsequent [offering] belongs to the Sviṣṭakṛt; therefore, one offers it in the northern half, for this is the direction of the Sviṣṭakṛt. This second oblation is offered for the sake of pairing, for a pair is indeed a couple.
Procreation (2.3.1). These two oblations are indeed these two:
the past and the future, the born and the yet to be born, the arrived and the yet to arrive.
Both hope and what is beyond hope—both these two are indeed the self;
for that which is the past is truly the self, and that which is the self is truly the past; offspring alone [are the future].
For that which is yet to be is indeed non-real; for that which is yet to be is non-real, and that which is progeny is the self.
That which has been born is indeed real; for that which has been born is real, and that which is the self is progeny.
For that which is yet to be born is uncertain; for that which is yet to be born is uncertain. Offspring is the self when it has arrived;
for that which has arrived is certain; for that which is the self is certain. Offspring is hope; for hope is uncertain.

In that respect, what is "addhā" (the manifest) is the progeny; for today is indeed manifest. And what is "anaddhā" (the unmanifest) is the self; for tomorrow is indeed unmanifest. Thus, what is manifest is the progeny, and what is unmanifest is the self. For today is manifest, and tomorrow is unmanifest.
