It is bound, just as progeny [is bound].
That which is the first oblation is offered for the sake of the self; one offers it with a mantra, for that which is a mantra is indeed manifest truth (*addhā*).

That which is the lower [oblation] is the self; then that which is the upper is offered for the sake of offspring. He offers it silently, for that which is silent is undefined, and that which is offspring is undefined. 2.3.1 [30] He offers: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! Then in the morning: "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"
By truth alone is the oblation offered. For when the sun sets, then Agni is the light; when the sun rises, then Sūrya is the light.
Indeed, that which is offered with truth goes to the gods. 2.3.1. [31] Now, a carpenter once said this to Āruṇi, who was desirous of spiritual luster: "Agni is luster; Sūrya is the light of luster."

"Radiance, light, radiance"—he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, indeed becomes possessed of Brahman-radiance. That [formula], "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā," is truly the form of procreation; it is light on both sides.
He takes up the seed with its deity; for seed, when taken up on both sides, is generated. Thus, having taken it up on both sides, he causes it to be generated. 2.3.1. [33] Now, in the morning.

"Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"—thus he encloses the seed on both sides with light by means of the deity; for seed that is enclosed on both sides is procreated. Having thus enclosed it on both sides, he brings it forth; that is the characteristic form of procreation. 2.3.1 [34]
Regarding this, Jīvala Cailaki said: "Āruṇi merely causes [the fire] to become an embryo; he does not bring it forth. One should therefore offer with this very [formula] in the evening. 2.3.1. [35]

Then in the morning: "Jyotis (light) is Sūrya; Sūrya is Jyotis, svāhā! He thus places the light outside as the deity for the seed; for seed that is born comes into being outside [the womb]; he thereby causes it to be born. 2.3.1. [36]
Regarding this they say: "In this way, one offers the sun into the fire at evening, and the fire into the sun at morning. Now, that is indeed the practice of those who offer after sunrise;

for when the sun sets, then the fire is the light, and when the sun rises, then the sun is the light. This [other method] is not a fault, but rather this very [method of ours] is a fault, in that the offering is not made directly to that specific deity.

In the case of the Agnihotra, where one offers with the formula, "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! there [one should not say], "To Agni, svāhā!"; and in the morning, where one offers with the formula, "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā! there [one should not say], "To Sūrya, svāhā!
One should offer using this very [formula]. 2.3.1. [37]

"With the god Savitṛ in harmony"—this is for the sake of impulsion by means of Savitṛ. "In harmony with Night, accompanied by Indra"—thereby he creates a union with Night; he makes it possessed of Indra, for Indra is the deity of the sacrifice. "May Agni, being pleased, accept [the offering], Svāhā!"—thereby he offers directly to Agni. 2.3.1. [38]

Then, in the morning: "In harmony with the god Savitṛ"—this contains the word *savitṛ* for the sake of impulsion; "in harmony with Uṣas, accompanied by Indra"—this refers either to the day or to the dawns;
he thus creates a union between the days and the dawns; he makes it "accompanied by Indra," for Indra is the deity of the sacrifice.
"May Sūrya, enjoying [it], come; Svāhā!"—thus he offers directly to Sūrya. Therefore, one should offer in this very manner.

They said, "Who will offer this for us? "A Brāhmaṇa indeed. "Brāhmaṇa, offer this for us. "What will be mine from that? "The remains of the Agnihotra itself. So, whatever he leaves remaining in the ladle...
Now, as for the remains of the *agnihotra* offering and what is left in the pot: just as one would pour out the remnants of a meal, so is that [the *agnihotra* remnant].
Therefore, anyone at all may drink it; however, a non-Brāhmaṇa should not drink it, for they place it over the fire. Therefore, a non-Brāhmaṇa should not drink it.
These deities indeed belong to whoever exists.
Indra, Yama the king, Naḍa the Naiṣidha, Anaśnan, Sāṃgamana, Asan, and Pāṃsava dwell in that [space].
Now, this very [sun] is indeed Indra.
The Āhavanīya fire is this very [sun]; the Gārhapatya fire is King Yama;
and the Anvāhāryapacana fire is Naḍa Naiṣidha. Because they bring him from the south day after day, therefore they say: "Day after day, Naḍa Naiṣidha leads King Yama from the south. 2.3.2. [3]

Now, that fire which is in the assembly hall is indeed the *anaśnantsāṃgamana* (the one who comes together with those who do not eat). Because they approach it even while fasting, therefore it is called *anaśnan*. And when they take away the ashes and scatter them, these are indeed the dust of the seat. He who knows this thus—thus [he knows].
"May these deities dwell here"—by this [thought], he indeed conquers all these worlds and traverses all the worlds. 2.3.2. [4] Their worship:
that which one performs when standing near and sitting near the Āhavanīya fire in the evening and in the morning, that indeed is it.

Now, as for its attendance: whatever he does after returning and sits or lies down by the Gārhapatya fire—that indeed is its attendance. Furthermore, whenever, while walking about, he remembers the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he should attend to it mentally; that indeed is its attendance. 2.3.2. [5]
Then, in the morning, having fasted and sat for a moment in the assembly hall, he may wander about at will; that itself is his attendance upon [the fire].
Or, wherever the removed ashes lie, he should approach that very spot; that itself is his attendance upon [the fire]. Thus it is.
These deities present themselves for laughter.
2.3.2.[6] The Gārhapatya fire indeed has the sacrificer as its deity; this one, however, has the rival as its deity.

Because it is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, therefore they should not carry it forward day by day; for indeed, those who, knowing this, do not carry it forward day by day, have no rivals. This [fire] is indeed the *anvāhāryapacana*. They should carry it forward only on the day of preparation (*upavasatha*).
Wherever they are about to sacrifice, there indeed this [fire] of his becomes brought for a purpose that is not in vain.
Or rather, they should bring it when the [sacrificial session] has concluded.

In that [milk] they should cook [the rice], and the Brāhmaṇas should eat it. If, however, one does not find that, he should tell [them] to place even the milk of a cow on the fire; in that [milk] he should tell [them] to cause the Brāhmaṇas to drink.
For those who act thus for one who knows this, his rivals indeed become worse off.
Therefore, one should desire to act in this very way. 2.3.2. [9] Now, when it has first been kindled, at that time it is as if it were smoking; it is then Rudra.

He who should desire, "May I eat food just as Rudra follows these creatures—sometimes with lack of faith, sometimes with violence, and sometimes with a blow"—he should then offer the oblation; for he who, knowing this, offers it at that time, indeed obtains such food. 2.3.2 [10]
Now, when it becomes especially bright,
then he indeed becomes Varuṇa. He who might desire,
"May Varuṇa attend upon these creatures as if seizing them, as if overpowering them, as if striking them down"— [for him this is the rite].

Thinking, "In this way may I obtain food," he should then offer the oblation; for he who, knowing this, offers the oblation at that time, indeed obtains that food. 2.3.2. [11] Now, when it becomes thus kindled—
The smoke rises high, crackling with supreme vigor; at that moment, he becomes Indra.

Therefore, if one should desire, "May I be like Indra in prosperity and glory," he should offer the oblation at that very time. He who, knowing this, offers it at that time, indeed obtains that food. 2.3.2. [12]
Now,
when the flame of one who is dying becomes as it were turned back or sideways and subsides, then he indeed becomes Mitra.
Therefore, if someone should desire, "May I eat this food with the friendliness of Mitra," regarding him they say, "This man is indeed [the friend of all]."

"He is a Brāhmaṇa and a friend; he harms no one at all"—thinking thus, he should then offer the oblation. He who, knowing this, offers the oblation at that time, indeed obtains this food. 2.3.2. [13] Now, when these embers appear as if shining...

Then he becomes a Brahman. He who should desire, "May I be endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas)," then indeed he should offer; for he who, knowing thus, offers at that time, attains this very food-eating power. 2.3.2. [14]
Of these, one should strive for one year.

Whether he himself offers the oblations or another offers them for him, if he offers them otherwise than prescribed, it is as if one who digs for water or seeks other food were to turn back midway; even so does he fail.
Now, as for him who offers together with another: just as one digging for water or some other kind of food would quickly strike it, so it is in that case.
For these oblations are indeed spades for obtaining food.
Verily, he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, cuts open for himself this very food-eating.
Now, as for that first oblation: 2.3.2 [16] [It is] that which is the first oblation.

Those [portions] which are the northern ones are the gods; those which are the southern ones are human beings; and that which he leaves remaining in the ladle is the cattle. He indeed offers the first oblation as it were in smaller measure.
He leaves as it were more in the ladle for the subsequent offering. 2.3.2.[18] As to why he offers the first oblation as it were less:
the gods are indeed fewer than human beings. And...

For more than half [of the offering] goes to the gods, since humans are indeed more numerous than the gods; and more than half he leaves remaining in the ladle, since cattle are more numerous than humans. Indeed, for one who, knowing this, performs the Agnihotra, his dependents become fewer while his cattle become more numerous; that is truly successful for him.
The wives were fewer, while the cattle were more numerous. 2.3.3.
[1] When Prajāpati created living beings, when he created Agni, that [Agni], once born, was indeed everything here.
They resolved to burn him, but they were unable to do so. Those who were the creatures at that time resolved to crush him;
but he, not enduring this, went toward a man.
He said: "I cannot endure this; come, let me enter you. Having begotten me from you, support me. He [the man] agreed.
"Just as you, having begotten me in this world, will maintain me, so shall I, having begotten you in that world, maintain you.
Saying "So be it," he begot him and maintained him. 2.3.3 [3] Now, when he establishes the sacred fires:
He thus procreates him; having procreated him, he sustains him.
Just as this [father] here in this world, having procreated him, sustains him, so indeed does this [Agni] there in yonder world, having procreated him, sustain him. 2.3.3. [4]
Therefore, one should not extinguish it prematurely;

for he who does so becomes weary prematurely, and just as he becomes weary prematurely for this world, even so does he become weary prematurely for that world. Therefore, one should not [extinguish it prematurely].
One should cause it to rise up together with [the fire].
Wherever he dies, wherever they place him upon the fire, there this one is born from the fire; he is this very son.
He becomes one whose father is still living. Therefore, this was declared by the seer:
"O gods, a hundred autumns are before us, within which you have brought about our old age."

"Wherein the sons become the fathers of their bodies, may he not harm our life-span in the midst of its course"—for he, being a son, becomes a father again; this is why one should establish the two fires.
That, indeed, is death.

This very one is the sun that shines. Since this one is indeed death, therefore those creatures that are on this side of it die; but those that are beyond it are the gods, and therefore they are immortal.
All these creatures are bound to his rays by their vital breaths; therefore the rays extend down toward the vital breaths.

Whomever he desires, taking away that person's vital breath, he rises up; that person dies. Indeed, whoever goes to yonder world without having escaped this Death, just as in this world one does not care for what is unrestrained when [Death] seizes it—so it is there.
Whenever he desires, then he causes death; in this very same way, he repeatedly causes death in that world.
When he offers two oblations in the evening after the sun has set—
By means of these two former feet, he stands firm upon this Death; then, when he offers two oblations in the morning before sunrise,
by means of these two latter feet, he stands firm upon this Death, and thus he [overcomes] him.
Rising, he rises taking it with him; thus he is released from death. This is the release from death in the Agnihotra.
Indeed, one who knows this release from death in the Agnihotra is released from repeated death. 2.3.3.
Just as the point of an arrow.
In this way, among sacrifices, the Agnihotra is like the point of an arrow; for by it one reaches the point of every arrow, and by this very means all his sacrificial rites have escaped this death.
Day and night, indeed, revolve in that world.

If they were to diminish a man's merit from this point backward for a day and night, then indeed his merit would not be diminished by that day and night. Just as one standing on the seat of a chariot...

When the two wheels of the chariot are revolving above, he should look down; thus, from beyond, he looks down upon this side, day and night. Day and night do not diminish the merit of him who knows this transcendence of day and night. 2.3.3 [13]
Having gone around the Āhavanīya fire from the east, he passes between the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya. The gods do not know a human being;
they know him as he passes between these two, thinking, "This one is indeed offering this to us. For Agni is the destroyer of evil.
"The two ascetics, the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya fires, having passed between them, have struck away evil; he, having struck away evil, becomes light itself through prosperity and fame. 2.3.3.
[14] Or rather, the door of the Agnihotra is to the north."
Just as one would enter by means of a door, so it is with that; but he who comes from the south and sits there, that is as if he were walking outside. This boat, indeed, leads to heaven.
That which is the Agnihotra belongs to this very boat that leads to heaven;
both the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya fires are its two hulls, and the milk-offerer is the oar. When he rows forward, it is thus.
2.3.3 [16] When he rows forward, it is thus.
Therefore, he anoints her facing eastward, toward the heavenly world; through her, he attains the heavenly world.

Her ascent is from the north; she thus brings him to completion in the heavenly world. Now, as for one who comes and sits to the south—just as if one were to come upon a ford that has already been crossed, he would be left behind and remain excluded from there; even so is it here.
Regarding that [TS 2.3.3.17]: Now, this kindling-stick which he places on the fire is a brick; the mantra with which he offers the oblation is the *yajus* with which he lays down this brick.
Indeed, whenever a brick is laid down, then an oblation is offered.
Therefore, these oblations which are the Agnihotra offerings are offered by him only upon those very bricks that have been laid down.
Prajāpati is indeed Agni;
Prajāpati is the year. Year after year, indeed...

For him who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, his Agnihotra is completed by means of the piled fire-altar; year after year he attains the piled fire-altar. Indeed, for him this Agnihotra is completed by means of the piled fire-altar, and he attains the piled fire-altar. 2.3.3 [19]
There are seven hundred and twenty Ṛg-verses; and when he offers the Agnihotra in the evening and in the morning, those two oblations become his oblations throughout the year. 2.3.3. [20]
Seven hundred and twenty; indeed,
year after year his Agnihotra becomes equal to the Great Hymn (mahad uktha), and year after year he attains the Great Hymn who knows thus.
The wise man offers the Agnihotra; this Agnihotra of his becomes united with the Great Hymn (mahad uktha), and he attains the Great Hymn. 2.3.4.
Indeed, the gods [offered it] in Agni.

They deposited all the animals, both those that are domestic and those that are wild, either intending to go forth for victory, or for the sake of acting according to their will, or thinking, "May this one,
the best protector, protect us. Agni, however, desired them for himself.
Having gathered them together, they entered the night, thinking, "Let us go back. The gods perceived that Agni had vanished; they realized, "He has indeed entered here; he has entered the night.
As the night was returning, they approached him in the evening, saying, "Give us our cattle; give us our cattle back!"

Agni gave the cattle back to them. For what purpose, then, should one pay homage to the two fires? Indeed, the two fires are the givers; it is to them that he makes this request. He should pay homage in the evening.

For in the evening the gods used to approach them; indeed, Datta bestows these two upon him who, knowing this, approaches them in the evening. Now, as to why one should not approach them: in the beginning, both the gods and humans existed here together. 2.3.4. [4] Then, as to why one should not approach them: in the beginning, both the gods and humans existed here together.

Whatever humans did not possess, they would ask for from the gods, saying, "This indeed we do not have; let this be ours. Out of resentment toward that very begging, the gods disappeared, thinking, "Lest I should cause harm; lest I should become hateful. Therefore, one should not perform the *upasthāna* (worship). 2.3.4 [5]

Now, as to why he should indeed stand near [the fire]: the sacrifice belongs to the gods, while the blessing belongs to the sacrificer; for this oblation is indeed the sacrifice, and it is the blessing that belongs to the sacrificer. Thus, by standing near [the fire], he secures for himself whatever belongs to him in this regard.
Therefore, one should indeed perform the *upasthāna* (homage). 2.3.4.
[6] Now, as to why one should not perform the *upasthāna*:
he who follows a Brāhmaṇa while praising him, or a Kṣatriya...
Thinking, "He will give to me" or "He will build a house for me," a person seeks to please someone either with wealth or with service;
indeed, that person considers it right to give to him. But he who says, "What are you to me, you who do not give to me?"—he may come to hate that person, or he may fall into despair.
Therefore, one should not perform ritual attendance (*upasthāna*). For when he kindles [the fire] and offers oblations, it is as if he were begging this very thing from him;
therefore, one should not perform ritual attendance. Now, as to why one should indeed perform ritual attendance:

Moreover, when one begs, one indeed obtains a giver; likewise, a husband does not always take notice of his wife. But as soon as she says, "I am indeed your wife; support me," then he knows her, and then he considers her his wife. Therefore, one should indeed perform this *upasthāna* (reverential salutation), for this is the complete whole of that for which one should perform the *upasthāna*. 2.3.4. [8]
Having become Prajāpati himself, he pours his seed— whatever he rules over and whatever follows him—
when he offers the Agnihotra; thus, by approaching it, he reproduces this entire world.
It brings forth everything. 2.3.4.[9] He begins with a verse containing the word *upa*. This earth is indeed *upa*; it is *upa* because of its duality, for whatever is born here is born upon it.

Whatever is offered in this [fire], that is produced in her; and whatever she consumes, that is consumed in her very self. Thus, by means of day and night, it becomes more and more inexhaustible. He thus enters upon this with that inexhaustible abundance. 2.3.4. [10] He says: "Approaching the sacrifice" (*upaprayanto adhvaram*). The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus he says, "approaching the sacrifice."

"We would utter the mantra unto Agni"—for he is about to speak this mantra to him—"hearing us from afar"—even if he is far away from us, he hears this; "just so, consider it thus"—this is what he says. 2.3.4.
[11] "Agni is the head of heaven."
"This Kakutpati quickens the seeds of the waters upon the earth"—thus he runs after it.
It is just as when a suitor might say something auspicious: "You are indeed the descendant of such-and-such; you are truly fit for this. Such is this [verse]. 2.3.4. [12]
Then [the verse] for Indra and Agni:

"O Indra and Agni, both of you I invoke; may you both rejoice together in the gift of wealth. Both of you are givers of food and riches; I call upon you both for the winning of booty. This, indeed, is Indra—he who shines yonder. He...

That which sets enters the Āhavanīya fire; thus he pays homage to both of them together, thinking, "May both of them, being together, grant [me boons]. Therefore, [the offering belongs] to Indra and Agni.
"This is your seasonal womb."
"Since you were born, O Agni, you proclaimed [it]; knowing that, ascend and then increase our wealth"—wealth indeed is nourishment; thus he says, "Make this nourishment for us more and more. 2.3.4.
[14] "This one here is the first."

He has been established by the creators as the Hotṛ-priest, the most excellent sacrificer, to be praised at the rites—he whom Apnavāna and the Bhṛgus caused to shine forth, the wonderful and pervasive one, for every clan. Thus he runs after [the sacrifice]. It is just as when a suitor speaks auspiciously, saying, "You are indeed the descendant of such-and-such; you are truly capable for this [task]"; even so is this [verse].
Thus he says this; when he says, "Pervading for every clan," it is because he indeed pervades every clan.
2.3.4.[15] "Following his ancient splendor, the bold ones have milked the bright milk from the seer who wins a thousandfold"—this is the supreme [verse].
This thousandfold gift is indeed the foremost of gifts; it is for the attainment of this very thing that he says, "The seer who wins a thousand with milk.
This is the six-verse hymn to be recited together.

Of that [hymn], the first verse contains the word "upavati" and the last contains the word "pratnavati. We have explained why it contains "upavati"; as for "pratna," that which was of old is indeed "adaḥ" (yonder). For as many gods as there were in the beginning, so many are the gods now;
therefore, that which was of old is "adaḥ. Between these two [verses] lie all desires; these two, being in agreement, bestow them upon us.
"He bends down all desires. He mutters the first verse three times and the last verse three times; for the commencement is threefold.
Sacrifices have threefold beginnings; therefore, one mutters the first verse thrice and the last verse thrice.
For indeed, when one here offers the Agnihotra, whether by speech or by action, it may become erroneous.
He does this for himself; he cuts away from his life, or from his luster, or from his progeny. 2.3.4. [19] And so it is said: "O Agni, you are the protector of the body;
protect my body. O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life. You are the giver of luster."

"O Agni, you are splendor; give me splendor. O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, that do you fulfill for me. (2.3.4.20) For indeed, when one here offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, whether by speech or by action, it may be performed erroneously.

"He cuts away from himself that [which belongs to him], whether it be from his life-span, or from his luster, or from his progeny; 'may that be replenished for me again,' this is what he thereby says. And so indeed, this of his is replenished again. 2.3.4. [21] "Kindling thee..."

"For a hundred winters we would kindle thee, the radiant one"—by this he means, "May we live for a hundred years. "So great as thou art, we would kindle thee"—this is what he means when he says, "the radiant one we would kindle. "Full of vigor, [we kindle] thee who art the maker of vigor; full of power, [we kindle] thee who art the maker of power"—by this he means, "We, being full of vigor..."
"May we be strength-makers; may you be a strength-maker"—this is what he says. "May we be possessed of power;

may you be a maker of power"—this is what he says. "O Agni, the subduer of rivals, may we, being undeceived, [attain] the undeceivable"—this is what he says: "Through you, may we make our rivals more wretched. 2.3.4 [22]

"O Citrāvasu, may you attain safety to the further shore. He mutters this three times. Citrāvasu is indeed the night, for she dwells as it were having gathered up the variegated things; therefore, no variegated thing is seen from the darkness. 2.3.4 [23]
By this means, indeed, the seers of old reached the safe end of the night;
by this means, the destructive spirits and demons did not find them during that night; and by this very means, he now reaches the safe end of the night.

By this he partakes of it; thus the destructive spirits and demons do not find him during the night. Standing, he mutters this much. 2.3.4. [24] Then, sitting down: "May you, O Agni, unite with the splendor of the sun. This he says because when the setting sun enters the Āhavanīya fire, he thereby refers to that. "With the hymn of the seers"—this he says because he stands worshipping (upasthāna). 2.3.4. [24] Then, sitting down: "May you, O Agni, unite with the splendor of the sun. [24] Then, sitting down: "May you, O Agni, unite with the splendor of the sun. This he says because when the setting sun enters the Āhavanīya fire
"May I unite with my beloved abode"—the oblations are indeed his beloved abode; thus he says this by means of the oblations.

"May I go united with life, united with luster, united with offspring, united with the increase of wealth"—just as you have united with these, so may I [unite] with life, luster, offspring, and the increase of wealth. As for the word "bhūman" (abundance): it is because he desires abundance.
"Thus, 'I shall associate with these,' this is what he says. 2.3.4 [25] Then he approaches the cows, saying: "You are food, may I enjoy your food; you are greatness, may I enjoy your greatness."

"Whatever energies are yours, whatever greatnesses are yours—may I partake of those from you," so he says; "you are strength, may I partake of your strength," so he says; "you are sap, may I partake of your sap," so he says; "you are abundance of wealth, may I partake of your abundance of wealth," so he says; "you are plenitude, may I partake of your plenitude," so he says. 2.3.4. [26]
"O wealthy ones, rejoice!"—for cattle are indeed wealthy; therefore he says, "O wealthy ones, rejoice.
"In this womb, in this stall, in this world, in this abode; stay right here, do not depart"—this he says for himself: "Do not depart from me at all. 2.3.4 [27]
Then he touches the cow, saying:
"Thou art united, possessing all forms. For cattle are, as it were, possessed of all forms;

therefore he says, "possessing all forms. When he says, "Enter me with vigor," he means "with sap"; and when he says, "with the lordship of cattle," he means "with the state of being a protector of cattle."
"He says 'with abundance'"; thus [it is said]. 2.3.4.[28] Then he approaches the *gārhapatya* fire.
He worships the *gārhapatya*: "O Agni, unto thee day by day..."

"May we, with minds free from fault, bring homage to him as he approaches. By saying "homage," one thus performs homage for him so that he may not harm him. 2.3.4 [29] "The ruler of the sacrifices..."

"The guardian of nectar, shining, increasing in his own home"—by saying "his own," he means "this which is mine"; thus he says, "Make this ours more and more. "As a father for his son... (2.3.4 [30])... for us.

"O Agni, be easy of access; be with us for our well-being"—by this he says: "Just as a father who is easy of access to his son does not harm him in any way, so be easy of access to us, and may we not harm you in any way. 2.3.4 [31]
Now the two-footed verses: O Agni, be our closest friend, our protector, and our auspicious shelter;
as the Vasu, Agni, of glorious fame, come hither and grant us most resplendent wealth—such as you are, O most radiant and shining one!
"Truly we pray for well-being for our friends; be mindful of us and hear our call. Protect us from every one who intends us harm.
(2.3.4 [32]) Or when he stands in attendance before the Āhavanīya fire.
He asks for cattle from him;

therefore, one worships him with various meters, for cattle are, as it were, of various kinds. Then, when he [asks] from the Gārhapatya fire for men, he does so with the first triplet, which is in the Gāyatrī meter, for the Gāyatrī is indeed man.
The metre of Agni is [the *gāyatrī*]; verily, by means of its own metre he approaches it. 2.3.4. [33] Now there are the two-footed verses.
The two-footed verse has man as its metre; for this man is indeed two-footed.
He does not indeed beg for men; rather, he begs for cattle. Therefore, those who have two feet are cattle.
He who, knowing this, performs the worship becomes possessed of cattle and possessed of men. Then he approaches the cow.
"O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come!"—for Iḍā is indeed the cow, and Aditi is indeed the cow; he touches her [with these words].

"Desirable ones, come!"—for human desires have entered into them; therefore he says, "Desirable ones, come! "May there be for me the fulfillment of your desires"—by this he means, "May I become dear to you. 2.3.4. [35]
Then, standing between the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires, facing eastward and looking at the fire, he mutters:
"O Brahmaṇaspati, make me a winner of Soma, like Kakṣīvat who was the son of Uśij; like him who is wealthy..."

"May he who removes disease, finds wealth, and increases prosperity—may he, the swift one, attend to us. May the curse of the stingy man, the malice of a mortal, not reach us. Protect us, O Brahmanaspati! (2.3.4).
Or rather, when he stands in worship before the Āhavanīya fire.

When he stands by the Āhavanīya fire, he thereby approaches heaven; and when [he stands] by the Gārhapatya, he thereby approaches the earth; and this [standing by the Dakṣiṇāgni] is the intermediate space, for this is the quarter of Bṛhaspati, and it is toward this quarter that he now approaches;
therefore, he mutters the Bārhaspatya formula. 2.3.4. [37]

May the protection of the three be great—the celestial favor of Mitra and Aryaman, and the unassailable power of Varuṇa. For over them, neither at home nor on distant paths, does the evil-speaking enemy have any mastery. For they are indeed the sons of Aditi.

"For the sake of the mortal who lives, they bestow eternal light"—this [verse] contains the words "not on the paths that ward off. Indeed, the paths that ward off are these [spaces] between heaven and earth; for he now stands upon them. Therefore he says, "not on the paths that ward off. 2.3.4. [38]
Then follows the verse addressed to Indra. Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; thus he makes this worship of Agni accompanied by Indra.
With the words, "Never art thou barren, O Indra, nor dost thou fail the donor," he means to say, "The donor is indeed the sacrificer; thou dost not harm the sacrificer.
And with the words, "Yea, O Maghavan, more and more does the gift of thee, the god, increase," [he praises him].
"Make this prosper more and more"—this is what he thereby says. 2.3.4.
[39] Now, the Sāvitrī: Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, all these [rites] for him are indeed impelled by Savitṛ.
"May our desires be fulfilled; we meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ, who shall impel our thoughts.
(2.3.4) Now follows the verse addressed to Agni: "He thus finally entrusts himself to Agni for protection: 'Thy [chariot], hard to overcome... (2.3.5)

"May the chariot reach us from every side, with which you protect the givers"—the givers are indeed the sacrificers. For with that chariot of his which is most invincible, he protects the sacrificers. "With that chariot of yours which is most invincible, with which you protect the sacrificers, with that protect us on all sides"—this is what he says.
He recites this three times (2.3.4.41).
Then he takes the name of his son, [saying],
"May this son of mine continue this vigor of mine," if he has a son.
It might even be that he would simply utter his own name. 2.4.1.1.
Then, when the *agnihotra* has been offered, he stands in worship, saying:
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. By means of this, he makes speech true.
When he says, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he invokes a blessing through that prosperity;
when he says, "May I be well-nourished with nourishments," he invokes prosperity.
Or rather, this long-standing ritual attendance upon the fire is itself [the invocation].
"That blessing is indeed this very blessing; by this much alone one obtains all this.
Therefore, one should worship with this alone. "This is precisely how we perform the service," so said Āsuri.
2.4.1 [3] Now, when about to depart on a journey...
First he worships the Gārhapatya fire, then the Āhavanīya.
He worships the Gārhapatya with the words,
"O manly one, protect my offspring," for it is this [fire] that rules over offspring.
He thus entrusts his offspring to him for protection.
Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire, saying:
"O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle! For he is the lord of cattle.
He thus entrusts him to the very cattle for their protection.
Then he either walks forward or causes [the cart] to run.
When he thinks it is the right time, having gone as far as that, he releases his speech.
Having departed and returned, he gazes at it; when he thinks the time is right, he restrains his speech.
Even if a king should be in between, he must not approach him. 2.4.1. [7] He first pays homage to the Āhavanīya fire.
Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire. The Gārhapatya is indeed the house; the house is indeed the foundation.
Thus, he establishes himself upon the house, upon that foundation. 2.4.1 [8] He then approaches the Āhavanīya fire.

"We have come to the all-knowing one, the best winner of wealth for us; O Agni, sovereign ruler, bestow upon us splendor and power. Having said this, he sits down and plucks away the grass-blades. Then he pays homage to the Gārhapatya fire.

"This Agni is the householder, the Gārhapatya, the best finder of wealth for his offspring. O Agni, householder, extend toward us splendor and strength! Having spoken thus, he sits down and plucks away the grass-blades; indeed, by means of this recitation, most people perform the worship in this very manner. 2.4.1. [10]

He should indeed remain silent. For when a superior person— whether a Brahmin or a king— resides with someone, it is simply not fitting for that person to say to him, "Protect this for me until I return."
"I shall dwell here"—but these superior gods, the fires, already dwell in this place; who then is fit to say to them, "Protect this for me, and then I shall dwell"?
For the gods indeed know the mind of a human being. 2.4.1 [11]
"He knows: 'The Gārhapatya has come to me for protection,'" thus he silently stands by the Āhavanīya fire, [thinking]: "He knows: 'The Āhavanīya has come to me for protection. 2.4.1. [12]
Then he either walks forward or causes [the horse] to run.
When he thinks it is the right time, having reached that point, he releases his speech.
Then, having gone abroad and looked back, when he thinks it is the right time, he restrains his speech—even if it be a king who intervenes.
It might be that he should not approach him at all.
2.4.1.[13] He first pays homage to the Āhavanīya fire, and then to the Gārhapatya.

He stands silently by the Āhavanīya fire; having sat down silently, he plucks away the grass blades. He stands silently by the Gārhapatya fire; having sat down silently, he plucks away the grass blades. 2.4.1. [14] Now, therefore, follows the ritual service for the house.
Now, when a householder has been away on a journey and has returned, his household members become as if terrified of him, thinking, "What will he say here?

What will he do? Those who say anything or do anything while he is there—the household members tremble before them, for they have the power to throw the family into disorder. But he who does not [say or do anything] there...

The beings indeed approached Prajāpati, saying, "Beings are indeed [your] offspring; ordain for us that by which we may live. Then the gods, having put on the sacrificial thread and bent their right knees, approached him; he said to them, "The sacrifice is yours."
"Food is your immortality, strength is yours, the sun is your light.
Then the ancestors, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and bending their left knees, sat down before him; he said to them, "Month by month for you..."
"May there be peace; *svadhā* be to you! The moon, swift as thought, is your light.
(2.4.2.3) Then men sat down around him, having covered their laps; he said to them, "In the evening and in the morning for you..."
"May there be food for you, death for you, Agni for you, and light for you.
Then the animals drew near to him; he made for them exactly what was suitable for themselves, whenever it might be that you [should eat].

"If you obtain [food], whether at the proper time or at an improper time, then eat it"—therefore, whenever they obtain it, whether at the proper time or at an improper time, they eat it. 2.4.2. [5] Now, they say that the Asuras also approached him constantly.
To them he gave darkness and illusion, saying, "This indeed shall be the Asura-illusion. But those creatures were indeed defeated;
these very creatures live even now just as Prajāpati had ordained for them. 2.4.2. [6]

Neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor animals transgress [this law]; only some humans transgress it. Therefore, whoever among men becomes fat with unwholesome things becomes fat with evil; he falls away, for falsehood does not lead to the higher path.

For by doing so, one becomes fat; therefore, one should indeed eat only in the evening and in the morning. He who, knowing this, eats only in the evening and in the morning, reaches his full span of life. Whatever he utters with speech, that indeed comes to pass, for he protects this divine truth. This, O Brahmin, is the section called "Radiance" (tejas), for one who is able to observe its vow. 2.4.2. [7]
This, indeed, is the case: when one gives to the ancestors month after month, it is at that very time—when he is seen neither in the east nor in the west—that he gives to them.
For this moon is King Soma, the food of the gods; on this night it wanes. When it has waned, he gives; thus he brings about concord among them. But if he were to give while it has not yet waned...
He should give it; he should make it equal for the gods and for the ancestors. Therefore, when this [sun] is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then he gives to them.
He indeed gives in the afternoon.
The forenoon belongs to the gods, the midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors; therefore, he gives [the gift] in the afternoon.
He [stands] behind the Gārhapatya fire.
Having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and being seated facing south, he takes this [grain].
Rising from that very spot, standing to the north of the Anvāhāryapacana fire and facing south, he threshes it. He cleans it once;
for the ancestors have departed once and for all, therefore he cleans it only once. 2.4.2. [10]

He cooks it. When it has been placed on the fire, he pours clarified butter (ājya) over it; for they offer oblations to the gods in the fire, they take up portions for humans, and this alone is for the ancestors; therefore, when it has been placed on the fire, he pours clarified butter over it. 2.4.2.[11]
Having taken it down from the fire, he offers two oblations to the gods.

For he who has established the sacred fires and performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices approaches the gods; yet, by this [offering], he has acted as if performing a sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña). Therefore...
Being impelled by the gods, he conceals this [act]; then he gives this to the ancestors. Therefore, having taken it out, he offers two oblations into the fire for the gods.
He indeed offers to Agni and to Soma.
When he offers to Agni, it is because Agni is indeed shared in all [sacrifices];
and when he offers to Soma, it is because Soma has the ancestors as his deity; therefore, he offers both to Agni and to Soma.
He offers in the fire with: "Svāhā to Agni, the bearer of the *kavya*! Svāhā to Soma, accompanied by the ancestors! 2.4.2. [13]

He places the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) on the fire; that is the portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt. Then, to the south of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he draws a line once; that is the portion for the altar (vedi).
For the ancestors have turned away once and for all; therefore, he draws the line only once. 2.4.2.
[14] Then he places a firebrand (ulmuka) beyond it.

If he were to give this to the ancestors without having placed the firebrand (ulmuka) down, the Asuras and Rakṣases would surely scatter them; but thus the Asuras and Rakṣases do not scatter the ancestors. Therefore, he places the firebrand down afterwards. 2.4.2 [15]
He deposits [the fire]:
"Those who, assuming various forms, being Asuras, move about by means of the *svadhā* offering;
those who carry away the *parāpur*s and the *nipur*s—may Agni drive them away from this world. For Agni is the repeller of the *rakṣases*.
Therefore, he deposits it in this manner.
2.4.2.[16] Then, taking a water-pot, he causes [the sacrificer] to wash his hands, saying to the sacrificer:
"O so-and-so, wash yourself!"
"O so-and-so, wash for your father; O so-and-so, wash for your grandfather; O so-and-so, wash for your great-grandfather.
Just as one would pour water over someone who is being consecrated, so it is in this case.
Then there are pieces of grass torn out once from the base of the roots.

It is indeed like the summit of the gods, like the middle of men, and like the root of the ancestors; therefore, the stalks are cut near the root. They are cut once, for the ancestors have departed once and for all; therefore, they are cut once. 2.4.2 [18]
He spreads them out toward the south;

there he gives. He gives, as it were, saying "sa vā" (he indeed). For they offer to the gods with "iti" (thus), they take up [the portion] for men, but for the ancestors it is done in this way; therefore he gives with "iti. 2.4.2.[19]
He gives [the gift], saying, "This, O so-and-so, is for your father. Regarding this, some say, "And for those who follow you"; however, one should not speak thus.
For he belongs together with them, and they belong together with him. Therefore, one should simply say:
"This, O so-and-so, is for your father," "This, O so-and-so, is for your grandfather," and "This, O so-and-so, is for your great-grandfather. Now, as for this...
He gives [the food] away, for the ancestors indeed turn away once and for all.
There he mutters:
"O ancestors, rejoice here; come to your respective portions like bulls."
"‘Eat according to your respective portions’—this is what he thereby says.
Then he turns away.
For the ancestors are, as it were, hidden from men; thus he becomes, as it were, hidden. He, indeed, [turns...]
"He has sat down exhausted," they say, "for such is the nature of an Asura. Having sat there for just a moment, he then turns around and mutters:
"The fathers have rejoiced; they have partaken according to their portions."
"He has partaken according to his share"—this is what he says by this.
Then, taking a vessel of water, he causes [them] to wash their hands;
for the sacrificer, he says, "O So-and-so, wash yourself."

"O so-and-so, wash for your father; O so-and-so, wash for your grandfather; O so-and-so, wash for your great-grandfather. This is just as if one were to sprinkle water upon someone who has already eaten. Then, having loosened the end of his garment, he pays homage.
The *nīvī* (the knot of the lower garment) indeed belongs to the ancestors; therefore, having loosened the *nīvī*, he pays homage.

Homage (*namaḥ*) is indeed the sacrifice; thus he makes them worthy of sacrifice. He pays homage six times, for there are six seasons, and the ancestors are the seasons; therefore he pays homage six times. "O ancestors, give us houses," he says; for [it is] of houses...
"O Fathers, may you rule over this; this is the blessing for this rite. Then he smells [the remains], having placed the *piṇḍas* back [on the fire];
that is the sacrificer's portion. He puts on the fire pieces of wood torn off once with his hand, and he also throws back the firebrand.
Regarding this, Kahoḍa Kauṣītaki said:
"Or rather, this is the essence of these two, heaven and earth;
having offered this essence to the gods, we shall then consume it. Therefore, one should indeed sacrifice with the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said:

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the Asuras smeared both kinds of plants—those upon which humans depend for their livelihood and those upon which cattle depend—with something like a magical spell (*kṛtyā*) and something like poison (*viṣa*), thinking, "In this way we shall surely overcome the gods. Consequently, neither humans nor cattle were affected by it.
Those golden offspring did not perish through fasting.
The gods heard of this: "Indeed, these offspring are perishing through fasting. They...

They said, "Come, let us strike this away from them!"—[the others asked], "By what means?"—"By the sacrifice alone. Indeed, by means of the sacrifice the gods and the seers brought about whatever prosperity they had.
They said, "To whom shall this belong among us? But they did not reach an agreement, each saying, "It shall be mine! It shall be mine! 2.4.3. [4]
Having made an agreement, they said, "Let us run a race in this [contest]; whoever among us wins shall possess this [world] of ours.
"So be it," they said, and they ran a race in it. Indra and Agni won.
Therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni;
for Indra and Agni won their portion for him. Wherever Indra and Agni stood after having conquered, there the All-Gods followed them. 2.4.3 [6]

Indra and Agni are the nobility (kṣatra), and the All-gods (viśve devāḥ) are the common people (viś). Wherever the nobility conquers, the common people are indeed included therein; so did Indra and Agni include the All-gods. Therefore, this oblation of cooked rice (caru) for the All-gods is offered. 2.4.3. [7]
"One should indeed offer that among the old [grains]," they say.
"Indra and Agni are the Kṣatra; let me not cause the Kṣatra to ascend further.
Both of them, however, should consist of new [grains], because one is a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and the other is a cooked rice offering (caru). It is by this very fact [that they are both new].
"The Kṣatra has not yet mounted them; therefore, both of these should belong to the Navas.
Then all the gods said:
"This essence of these two, Heaven and Earth—come now, let us..."
"Let us share in this," they said; for them they assigned this portion, this cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
Therefore there is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. This earth itself is its potsherd, for this [earth] is indeed one; therefore it is offered on one potsherd. 2.4.3. [9]
This is the criticism of it: for whatever deity the oblation is taken, the Sviṣṭakṛt is everywhere entitled to a share;
yet here he offers all of it and does not cut off a portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt—that is the criticism.
"The oblation turns back.

Regarding this, they say: "This cake on one potsherd has turned back; it will bewilder the kingdom. This is not a matter for concern, for the Āhavanīya fire is the foundation of oblations. Even if [the oblation] reaches the Āhavanīya ten times over, [it remains established there].

One should not turn back nor heed what others say; for who would enter into an agreement with them? Therefore, one should sacrifice only with clarified butter (*ājya*). Indeed, clarified butter is the manifest essence (*rasa*) of these two, heaven and earth; thus, he directly gratifies them with their own essence, their own sacrificial food.

Therefore, one should sacrifice with clarified butter alone. By means of this very sacrifice, the gods, having sacrificed, [obtained] both kinds of plants— those upon which humans subsist and those [upon which other beings subsist].
The cattle smote away the *kṛtyā* as it were, and the poison as it were, from him; then men ate [the meat] and the cattle licked [it]. 2.4.3.
Now, when he sacrifices with this [offering], truly no one at all treats him as if with a *kṛtyā* or as if with poison.
"He anoints you," he says; "the gods did so"—it is indeed this that he does here. And whatever portion the gods assigned to themselves, that very portion he now assigns to them.
Furthermore, both kinds of plants—those upon which humans subsist and those upon which cattle subsist—he thereby makes free from disease.
He makes them free from blemish; these creatures, being free from disease and free from blemish, subsist upon them. Therefore, indeed, he performs this sacrifice with this [offering].
A cow born first is its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
For this is indeed the foremost [offering].

If he has already performed sacrifices, he should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices and then sacrifice with this; but if he has not yet performed sacrifices, they should cook this four-fold portion of boiled rice on the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and the Brāhmaṇas should eat it. 2.4.3. [14]

There are indeed two kinds of gods: the gods who are the gods themselves, and those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred lore—they are the human gods. Just as an oblation is offered when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, so does this [offering] become for him; therein—

If one should ask for it, he should give it; [but] it should not be a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for they say that it would be an oblation (*havis*). One should not offer it in the *agnihotra*, for he would thereby cause a conflict (*samada*).
If he were to offer it in the *agnihotra*, the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice would be one thing and the *agnihotra* another; therefore, he should not offer it in the *agnihotra*. 2.4.4.1.

Prajāpati, indeed, performed this sacrifice first, desiring offspring, [thinking]: "May I be many through offspring and cattle; may I attain prosperity; may I have glory; may I be an eater of food. 2.4.4. [2]
He was indeed named Dakṣa; because he performed this sacrifice first, it is therefore called the Dākṣāyaṇayajña.
Some, however, call it the Vasiṣṭhayajña, for Vasiṣṭha is indeed this very one.

Regarding this they say: "He performed this sacrifice; having performed this sacrifice, he became that which is this progeny and glory of Prajāpati. Verily, he who, knowing thus, performs this sacrifice, procreates that same progeny and attains that same glory. Therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice. 2.4.4. [3]
Thereupon, Pratīdarśa Śvekna performed that sacrifice. For those who opposed him, it was as if there were a dispute;
indeed, for one who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, there is as if a dispute. Therefore, one should perform this sacrifice.
"One should sacrifice.
Suplan Sārñjaya came to him; from him he learned this sacrifice and another as well. He practiced the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) under him.
Having recited [the hymns], he went again to the Sṛñjayas. Those Sṛñjayas recognized him, saying, "He has come after reciting our sacrifice.

They said, "He has indeed come to us together with the gods, since he has come after reciting our sacrifice. He was Sahadeva Sārñjaya. There is also this very saying: "Or rather, he gave another name to the enemy, [calling him] Suplā. By means of this...

He performed this sacrifice; having sacrificed with it, that progeny and that prosperity which belongs to the Sṛñjayas came into being. Indeed, he who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, procreates such progeny and attains such prosperity;
therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice. It was with this that he then sacrificed.

Devabhāga Śrautarṣa was the domestic priest (*purohita*) of both the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas; indeed, that is the highest position (*paramatā*). Truly, even he who is the domestic priest of a single kingdom holds a high position;
how much more so he who [is priest] of two? He who knows this and acts accordingly attains, as it were, the highest position.
One sacrifices with a sacrifice; therefore, one should indeed sacrifice with this [rite].
With it, Dakṣa Pārvati once sacrificed; even now, these Dākṣāyaṇas have attained as it were sovereignty.

He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with this [rite], indeed obtains sovereignty here; therefore, one should sacrifice with this. Each cake (puroḍāśa) is offered on successive days; by this, his prosperity becomes free from rivals and unassailable. He sacrifices at two full-moon festivals and two new-moon festivals. Two indeed constitute a pair; thus, it is a productive pair.
It is performed. 2.4.4.[7] Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the Agniṣomīya on the day before the full moon: those two deities are two; indeed, they are two.
A pair is indeed thus produced as a means of procreation. 2.4.4.
[8] Then, in the morning: there is a cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni and the Sāṃnāyya offering for Indra; these are two deities, for two indeed...
A pair is indeed created as a productive couple.
Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Indra and Agni on the day before the new moon: those two deities constitute a pair, for a pair consists of two.
Thus, this very pair is produced for the sake of procreation. Then, in the morning,
there is a cake for Agni and a curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa, [thinking], "Lest I depart from the sacrifice."

Now, the cake for Agni is indeed one deity, whereas these two, Mitra and Varuṇa, are two deities; two indeed constitute a pair, and thus a productive pair is created. This is that form of his by which he becomes manifold, by which he procreates. 2.4.4. [11]

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Agni and Soma on the day before the full moon: that very same animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma which he performs on the fast-day is indeed his [the second one]. 2.4.4. [12]
Then, in the morning, there is a cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni and the Sāṃnāyya offering for Indra.
Of this [sacrifice], the cake for Agni is indeed the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), for the morning pressing belongs to Agni; and that which is for Indra is the midday pressing.
The *sāṃnāyya* offering is his midday pressing, for the midday pressing belongs to Indra. Then,
as for the fact that he sacrifices with the *aindrāgna* [oblation] on the previous day at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), that is his third pressing.
That third pressing indeed belongs to the Viśvedevas, for Indra and Agni are the Viśvedevas.
Now, in the morning:
there is a cake for Agni and curds for Mitra and Varuṇa, [thinking], "Lest I depart from the sacrifice."

Now, there is indeed no cake for Agni; rather, that very cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa which he seizes as the *anūbandhyā* (the animal to be bound after the sacrifice) is his curd-offering (*payasyā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having performed the Full-moon and New-moon sacrifices, he conquers as much as he would conquer by performing the Soma sacrifice; thus, indeed, it becomes a great sacrifice. 2.4.4. [15]

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Agni and Soma on the day before the full moon: it was by this very [offering] that Indra slew Vṛtra, and by this very [offering] he won that victory which is his; in the same way, this sacrificer likewise [conquers] evil by means of this [offering].

It slays the hating rival and likewise conquers; now, as for why he prepares the *sāṃnāyya*—the *sāṃnāyya* belongs to the new moon (*amāvāsya*), and that which is called "new moon" is far away. It was with this essence that they gratified Indra after he had slain Vṛtra; indeed, he who, knowing this, performs [the sacrifice] on the full moon day, swiftly casts off evil.
He brings it together. This King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, which is the moon.
On the previous day they press him out, intending to consume him in the morning; thus they consume that part of him which has waned. 2.4.4 [16]

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Agni and Soma on the day before the full moon: he thereby presses him [Soma]; into that which has been pressed, he places this essence by means of this [offering].
He makes it pungent with juice; indeed, he makes the oblation savory for the gods, and his oblation becomes savory for the gods, who, knowing this, prepares the *saṃnaya* on the full-moon day.
Now, as for that which is done on the previous day...

He sacrifices with the offering to Indra and Agni on the new moon day; for Indra and Agni are indeed the two deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. It is to these two that he thus sacrifices directly and perceptibly. Indeed, the New and Full Moon sacrifices have been truly performed by him who knows this. 2.4.4. [18]

Then, in the morning, there is a cake for Agni and a dish of curds for Mitra and Varuṇa. The cake for Agni is indeed [offered] so that he may not depart from the sacrifice; and these two half-months are Mitra and Varuṇa—that which waxes is Varuṇa.

He who wanes is the friend; on this night both meet together, and thus, being together, he gratifies them both. Indeed, everything becomes gratified for him and everything is attained by one who knows this thus. On that very night— 2.4.4 [19]—he does so.
Mitra pours forth seed into Varuṇa; by that seed he is procreated when [the moon] is filled.
Therefore, the curdled milk (payasyā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is most appropriately prepared here.
Indeed, the new moon (amāvāsyā) is the occasion for the Sāṃnāyya offering.

Therefore, this is performed on the full-moon day. For if he were to prepare the *saṃnāyya* (the mixture of curds and milk) even on that occasion, he would commit a redundancy and cause a conflict; thus, having gathered him from the waters and the plants, he causes him to be born from the oblations.
Having been born from the oblations, he is seen afterwards. 2.4.4. [21]
He thus causes him to be born from this very union: the *payasyā* is the female and the *vājina* is the seed;
for whatever is born from a union is born immediately therefrom, and so he causes him to be born from this procreative union. Therefore, this [offering] occurs here.
There is curdled milk (payasyā).
Then he offers the whey (vājina) to the Vājins.
The seasons indeed are the Vājins, and the whey is seed; thus he places that seed in its proper order.
The seasons pour forth seed; once poured, these creatures bring it forth. Therefore, one offers the *vājina* (curdled milk) to the *vājins* (the swift ones).
He indeed offers as if from behind the sacrifice;
for having approached from behind, the bull mounts the female. In her—
He pours out the seed; indeed, he first offers it beforehand with "O Agni, accept! and performs the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, which is the portion for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. He offers it beforehand.
Then he sprinkles the quarters.

"To the quarters, to the intermediate quarters, to the directed quarters, to the sub-quarters, to the upward quarters, svāhā to the quarters!"—thus there are five quarters and five seasons; by means of the seasons, he thus brings about union with the quarters.
Regarding this, they consume [the food] in five portions.

The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Āgnīdhra, and the sacrificer—these are five, for there are five seasons; thus the form of the seasons is produced. He thereby establishes that seed, once poured, within the seasons.
The first sacrificer eats [of the remains], thinking, "May I first grasp the seed"; and likewise the last one.
"May the seed be established in me, the highest; being invited, invite [it]. By saying this, they indeed make it Soma. 2.5.1.
Prajāpati, verily, was here alone in the beginning. He reflected: "How indeed might I be propagated? He exerted himself. He...
He performed austerity; he created offspring. Once created, those offspring of his perished; they became these very birds.
Man indeed is nearest to Prajāpati, for man is two-footed; therefore birds are two-footed.
Then Prajāpati reflected.

"Just as indeed I was alone before, so indeed am I now all alone," he thought; thus he created a second [being], but they vanished from him. That became this small crawling thing which is other than snakes.
"He created a third," they say; they also vanished from him, and they became these snakes. These indeed...
"Is it not indeed twofold? Yājñavalkya said, "But rather, it is threefold: the Ṛg, the Yajus, and the Sāman.
Prajāpati, chanting and exerting himself, reflected:
"Why is it that my created beings perish?"
He perceived this very thing: "It is indeed through lack of food that my creatures are perishing.
He first caused milk to swell in his own breasts; he created creatures, and those creatures of his, once created, reached toward his breasts and from that they flourished.
These are the ones who have not perished. 2.5.1 [4]
Therefore, this was declared by the Seer: "Three generations have passed away. By this, he refers to those that perished.
Then he says, "Others have settled around the *arka*. The *arka*, indeed, is Agni; thus, he refers to these present generations.
Those [gods], having not been defeated, sat down around the fire; it is with reference to them that this was recited:
"Great indeed he stood within the worlds"—this was recited with reference to Prajāpati as Pavamāna.
"He has entered the green ones"—the quarters are indeed the green ones, and this purifying wind has entered them; that very verse was recited concerning them.
These creatures are produced in the same manner as Prajāpati produced creatures. For when the breasts of a woman swell, and the udder of cattle, then what is born is born from those.
Having reached the breasts, they come into being.
That [breast milk] is indeed food;
for it was this that Prajāpati first produced as food. And that food is indeed progeny.
For from food this [universe] comes into being; for those [cows] whose milk there is, they come into being after reaching the two udders;
and those whose milk there is not, they eat them as soon as they are born. Thus, even they come into being from food alone. Therefore, food indeed is offspring. 2.5.1. [7]
He who desires offspring, by sacrificing with this oblation, ordains for himself the sacrifice as Prajāpati come into being. 2.5.1. [8]
That cake on eight potsherds is indeed for Agni.
Agni is the mouth of the gods and the progenitor; he is Prajāpati. Therefore, it is for Agni. 2.5.1. [9]
Now there is a Soma oblation; Soma is indeed seed. Thus he pours Soma, the seed, into Agni, the procreator;
that is a productive union at the beginning. 2.5.1. [10]
Now follows the offering to Savitṛ:

there is a sacrificial cake on twelve potsherds or on eight potsherds. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods, and Prajāpati is the progenitor from the middle; therefore, it belongs to Savitṛ. 2.5.1. [11]
Then there is a pap for Sarasvatī and a pap for Pūṣan. Sarasvatī is indeed a female and Pūṣan is a male;
that is a productive couple. From this twofold productive couple, Prajāpati [arose].

He created offspring from here upwards and from there downwards; and so indeed does he now create offspring from this very same twofold generative union, from here upwards and from there downwards. Therefore, these five oblations come into being.
Now, therefore, follows the locus of the *payasyā* offering.
There is a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts; the Maruts are indeed the clans, the clans of the gods.
They moved about here as if unrestrained. They approached Prajāpati, who was performing the sacrifice, and said: "Your [sacrifice] is indeed deficient."
"We shall destroy these creatures whom you will create with this oblation," [he said]. Prajāpati reflected:
"My former creatures have perished; if these ones also destroy them, then..."
Thinking, "Something will still remain over," he assigned this portion to them: this cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts.
This is that cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts. As to why it is on seven potsherds—it is because the host of the Maruts consists of sevens;
therefore, there is a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts. 2.5.1. [14]
One should indeed perform it with the verse "To them, the self-strong ones.

For they themselves made this their portion; thus, for those who do not find the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses addressed to the self-strong ones, this [offering] should indeed be for the Maruts. This is for the sake of non-injury toward living beings.
Therefore, the wind is produced. 2.5.1.[15] Now, therefore, concerning the *payasyā* (curd-mixture) itself:
from milk indeed creatures come into being; they are born from milk. Therefore...
From whatever they have arisen, that very thing he now brings about for them; those creatures which he creates by means of the previous oblations arise from this milk, from this *payasyā*.
In that [mixture], there is a pairing.

The woman is the milk-curd, the seed is the whey; from that union everything immeasurable was produced. Since everything immeasurable was produced from that union, therefore it belongs to the Viśvedevas. 2.5.1. [17]
Now there is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
By means of these oblations, Prajāpati, having created living beings, enclosed them within Heaven and Earth;
thus these [beings] are enclosed by Heaven and Earth. And so it is here.
Thus, when he creates offspring by means of these oblations, he encompasses them with heaven and earth;
therefore, there is a cake on one potsherd for heaven and earth. Now, therefore, follows the ritual procedure.
They do not strew the high altar (uttaravedi), thinking, "What is released is non-existent; the Vaiśvadeva is non-existent; it is non-existent.
The sacrificial grass (barhis) is tied together in three parts, but that is again made into one; for this is the form of procreation. Indeed, this is procreation:
the father, the mother, and what is born is the third. Therefore, though being threefold, it is again made into one.
The sacrificial grass-bunches (*prasū*) are tied together; he takes that as the *prastara* (grass-bundle).
For this is procreation, and the *prasū* is indeed procreation; therefore, he takes the *prastara* from the *prasū*.
Having set down the oblations, they churn the fire.
Indeed, when Agni was being born, the creatures of Prajāpati were born after him;
and in the same way, when this [sacrificer's] Agni is being born, the creatures are born after him. Therefore, having set out the oblations, they churn the fire. 2.5.1. [20]
There are nine fore-offerings;

there are nine after-offerings. The Virāj indeed consists of ten syllables; thus he makes this Virāj deficient on both sides for the sake of procreation. From this very procreative source, which is deficient on both sides, Prajāpati produced all creatures.

He created offspring from here upwards and from there downwards; even so does he now create offspring from this deficient source of generation both from here upwards and from there downwards. Therefore, there are nine fore-offerings (prayājas) and nine after-offerings (anuyājas). 2.5.1. [21]

There are three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations; for this sacrifice is, as it were, superior to the ordinary *havis*-sacrifice in that it has nine *prayājas* and nine *anuyājas*. Moreover, there may be only one [such oblation], for it is a *havis*-sacrifice; its sacrificial fee is a first-born cow. 2.5.1. [22]
By means of this very sacrifice, Prajāpati sacrificed;
that which is the offspring of Prajāpati and that which is his glory—this he became.
Verily, he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with this sacrifice, procreates that same offspring and attains that same glory.
Therefore, one should indeed sacrifice with this. 2.5.2.
Prajāpati created offspring by means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; those offspring of his, once created, [fell] to Varuṇa.
As many as they ate—barley indeed belongs to Varuṇa at the beginning;
because Varuṇa seized those very barley grains, therefore they are called the Varuṇapraghāsas.
Varuṇa seized them.
Seized by Varuṇa, they became dilated; some breathed out and some breathed in, and they lay down and sat up.

Indeed, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the up-breath (*udāna*) did not depart from them, but all the other deities departed. It was because of those two alone that his offspring did not perish. 2.5.2. [3]
With this oblation Prajāpati healed himself;
both his offspring that were already born and those that were yet unborn he released from Varuṇa’s noose, and thus his offspring were born free from disease and free from blemish. 2.5.2 [4]
Now, as to why he performs these sacrifices in the fourth month:
it is not that Varuna seizes his offspring in that manner;
rather, he does this because the gods did so, and thus he does the same for both his offspring that have been born and those yet unborn.
He releases both [types of offspring] from Varuna’s noose; thus his offspring are born free from disease and free from blemish.
Therefore, indeed, he performs these sacrifices in the fourth month. In that regard, there are two altars and two fires.
Now, as to why there are two altars and two fires:
it is from both sides that he thus releases the creatures from Varuna’s noose—from here upwards and from there downwards; therefore there are two altars and two fires.

He scatters the Uttaravedi only on the northern altar, not on the southern one; for Varuṇa is the nobility (kṣatra) and the Maruts are the common people (viś). He thus places the nobility above the common people; therefore, [the king] sits upon it.
These subjects wait upon the Kṣatriya from below; therefore, one scatters the Uttaravedi only on the northern side, not on the southern. Now, there are these very five oblations.
By means of these very oblations Prajāpati created offspring;
by means of them he released the offspring from Varuṇa’s noose on both sides—from here upwards and from there downwards.
Therefore, indeed, there are these five oblations. 2.5.2 [8]
Then there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni.
Indra and Agni are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath;
just as one would perform a good deed for someone who has done a good deed, so it is with this: for that reason, his offspring do not [perish].
They were overcome; by means of this [offering], he heals the creatures through the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the up-breath (*udāna*), and he places the out-breath and up-breath within the creatures.
Therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni. In both cases, there are two milk-offerings (*payasyā*).

Beings indeed originate from milk; once originated from milk, they remain so. Therefore, from that very source from which they were born and from which they originate, he thereby releases these offspring from Varuṇa’s noose on both sides—from above here and from below here. That is why there are curd-offerings on both occasions.
Regarding the two verses for Varuṇa (2.5.2.[10]):
the subsequent verse belongs to Varuṇa;
for it was Varuṇa who seized his offspring—this is the direct evidence.
He releases creatures from Varuna’s noose by means of the offering to the Maruts on the south; indeed, it is for the sake of non-repetition that there is an offering to the Maruts on the south.
For he would commit repetition if both offerings were to Varuna. Moreover, the Maruts sought to destroy his offspring from the south;
he appeased them with this share, and therefore there is an offering to the Maruts on the south. 2.5.2. [11]
He scatters *karīra* fruits for both of them.
Prajāpati indeed created comfort (*kaṃ*) for his creatures by means of the *karīra* fruits;
verily, this sacrificer now creates comfort for his creatures. 2.5.2 [12]
Of both of them he strews *śamī* leaves and *palāśa* leaves.
Prajāpati indeed made peace for his offspring with *śamī* leaves and *palāśa* leaves; verily, he now makes peace for these offspring. 2.5.2. [13]
Now, there is a cake on one potsherd for Kāya.

Prajāpati indeed created comfort (*kaṃ*) for his creatures by means of this cake on one potsherd for Kāya; verily, this sacrificer now creates comfort for his creatures by means of this cake on one potsherd for Kāya.
He performs [the rite] with a *puroḍāśa*; therefore, there is a single-cupcake (*ekakapāla*) *puroḍāśa* for Ka. 2.5.2.
[14] Then, on the previous day, having husked barley grains as it were on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire and having heated them slightly, of those—
They prepare vessels of *karambha* (barley meal mixed with curds), as many as there are members of the household, plus one additional;
in those, they also fashion a ram and a ewe. If, upon that ram and that ewe, wool other than that of a sheep (*anaida-kī*) is found—
Having found them, he should wash them and attach them; if he should not find those made of sheep's wool, then they may even be made of *kuśī* grass.
Now, as for why there is both a ram and a ewe:
this is indeed Varuṇa manifest before one's eyes.

The animal is a ram; he thereby visibly releases offspring from Varuna’s noose. They are made of barley, for Varuna seized the offspring when they had eaten barley. They are a pair, and thus he releases offspring from Varuna’s noose by means of a pair. 2.5.2 [17]
He places a ewe in the northern milk-mixture and a ram in the southern; for thus is a pair properly formed, since the woman lies on the left side of the man.

The Adhvaryu places all the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) upon the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), and then the Pratiprasthātṛ places this very *payasyā* (curd-mixture) upon the southern altar (*dakṣiṇavedi*). 2.5.2 [19]
Having placed the oblations, he churns the fire;
having churned the fire and cast it into the hearth, he makes an offering over it. Then the Adhvaryu says, "Recite for the fire being kindled!
Both of them then place fuel on the fire, both leave two kindling-sticks remaining, and both [perform the same actions].

While the two of them are pouring the two prior *āghāra* libations, the Adhvaryu alone says, "O Agnīdh, sweep the fire! Even though this has been thus commanded, it remains as if unswept. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ returns.

When he is about to lead his wife away, he asks, "With whom do you consort? For a woman commits an offense against Varuṇa when she consorts with another while belonging to one; furthermore, [he asks] lest she should offer the oblation with a thorn still within her. Therefore he asks. Indeed, a sin becomes less manifest when it is spoken; for it becomes truth. For this reason also he asks. She—
Whatever he does not promise to his kinsmen, that will surely be harmful to him. (2.5.2.21) He makes her recite:
"We invoke the Maruts, the devourers, who destroy the enemy, who are well-pleased with the groats. (2.5.2.21)

Just as with the *puro'nuvākya*, so too does he summon them from these vessels by means of this [verse]. 2.5.2. [22] These [vessels] indeed correspond to the number of persons; however many householders there may be, there are that many [vessels], with one in excess.

Thus, for each individual person, with one [verse] he releases from the noose of Varuṇa those offspring of his that have been born; with one [verse] there are extra [verses], and so he releases from the noose of Varuṇa those offspring of his that are yet unborn; therefore there are one extra [verses]. 2.5.2. [23]

The vessels are made of barley; for it is in vessels that food is eaten, and they are made of barley because Varuṇa seized the creatures after they had eaten barley. He offers with a winnowing basket, for with a winnowing basket food is prepared. The wife offers; thus he releases the offspring from the noose of Varuṇa by means of a pair. 2.5.2 [24]
He offers before the sacrifice, before the oblations;
for the subjects (*viś*) are indeed consumers of unoffered food, and the Maruts are the subjects.
When the creatures of Prajāpati were seized by Varuṇa, they were torn asunder and lay prostrate—some breathing and some not, some lying down and some sitting.
The Maruts then struck away the evil from those women; in the same way, the Maruts strike away the evil from his offspring.
Therefore, he offers before the sacrifice and before the oblations.
He indeed offers in the southern fire.

"Whatever in the village, whatever in the forest"—for sin is committed both in the village and in the forest; "whatever in the assembly, whatever in the senses"—by "whatever in the assembly," he means "whatever among men"; by "whatever in the senses," he means "whatever among the gods. "Whatever sin we have committed, this we expiate with 'Svāhā!'"—whatever [it may be].
"May we not suffer harm from this; may we be released from all of that"—this is what he says.
Then he mutters the verse addressed to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
For when the Maruts [struck] the evil of Prajāpati’s creatures—
They then disturbed his insight, thinking, "May these subjects of mine not disturb us. He muttered this verse addressed to Indra accompanied by the Maruts;
for Indra is the nobility (*kṣatra*) and the Maruts are the common people (*viś*), and the nobility indeed [protects] the common people.

The prohibitor has prohibited [him], saying "he is non-existent"; therefore, it belongs to Indra (aindrī). "O Indra, do not [forsake] us here in battles with the gods; for indeed, O impetuous one, there exists your great portion.
The song of the Maruts, who possess oblations, praises the bountiful one whose youthful power is great. (RV 2.5.2.28–29)
Then he makes her recite: "The doers of the rite have performed the rite"— for indeed the doers of the rite have performed the rite— "together with speech, bringing bliss"—
for indeed they performed it together with speech— "having done the rite for the gods, to the setting"— for indeed, having done the rite for the gods, [they went] to the setting.
"Come together, O spirits," he says; for they come together with one who has been married from another [family]. Therefore he says, "come together. "Go to your home," he says;
for this wife is indeed the hind part of the sacrifice. He has thus caused her to sit facing eastward toward the sacrifice.
The home is the "home" (asta); the home is the foundation. Thus, he establishes her in the home, in that very foundation. 2.5.2. [30]
The Pratiprasthātṛ comes out having carried [the oblation] back.
They sweep the fire; once the fire has been swept, both of them pour the two northern Āghāra-libations. Then the Adhvaryu alone, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, chooses the Hotṛ; he being chosen—
The Hotṛ sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat to the north of the northern altar; having sat down, he gives the impulse. Both, being thus impelled, take up the two offering-spoons and step across.
