Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*.
At every fourth *prayāja* offering, they both pour together [the butter]; they perform nine *prayāja* offerings. 2.5.2. [31]
Then the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite for Agni.

Both of them, having taken four portions of clarified butter each for the Ājyabhāga offering to Agni, step across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and both of them [respond].
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, they both offer. 2.5.2.
[32] Then the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite for Soma";
both of them [recite] the *saumya ājyabhāga*.

Having taken four portions of clarified butter and stepped across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Sacrifice to Soma! Then both of them offer the oblation at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*. 2.5.2.
[33] Now, whatever is to be performed by speech—
The Adhvaryu alone performs that, not the Pratiprasthātṛ;
thus, it is the Adhvaryu alone who calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* here, where the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
The Pratiprasthātṛ merely imitates what has been done.

Varuṇa is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*) and the Maruts are the common people (*viś*); thus he makes the common people follow after the nobility, acting in accordance with its will and following its path.
For if the Pratiprasthātṛ were also to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he would make the common people rebellious toward the nobility; therefore, he does not do so.
The Pratiprasthātṛ causes the announcement to be made.
2.5.2.[35] The Pratiprasthātṛ is indeed the vital breaths; having taken up the two offering-spoons, he waits, while the Adhvaryu alone [proceeds] with these oblations.

He proceeds with a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve or eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni. 2.5.2 [36]
Then, intending to proceed with these two milk-offerings (payasyā), they exchange them:
that which is the ram for the offering to the Maruts, he places it in the vessel for Varuṇa; and that which is the ewe for the offering to Varuṇa, [he places it in the vessel for the Maruts].
He places it in the northern direction. As for why they carry it around in this manner: Varuṇa is indeed the Kṣatra (the ruling power), and the man is vigor;

thus they place vigor in the Kṣatra. The woman is indeed without vigor, and the Maruts are the Viś (the common people); thus they make the Viś without vigor. That is why they carry it around in this manner. 2.5.2 [37]
Then the Adhvaryu himself says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Varuṇa.
He spreads a layer of clarified butter [into the ladle], and then he cuts off two portions from this curd-mixture dedicated to Varuṇa; he does this together with one of the other portions.

He places the ram [on the fire], then pours clarified butter over it from above, anoints the two portions of the offering, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Varuṇa! and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 2.5.2.
[38] The Adhvaryu holds [the vessel] in his left hand.

Having prepared the two *sruva*-ladles, the Adhvaryu, having taken hold of the Pratiprasthātṛ from the south, says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts. The Pratiprasthātṛ spreads a base of clarified butter (*ājya*) and then makes two cuttings from this curd-mixture for the Maruts; he does so together with one of the other portions.
He places the ewe; then he pours clarified butter over it from above, anoints the two portions of the offering, and steps across.
Then the Adhvaryu himself, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, says, "Recite the offering-verse for the Maruts," and he makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 2.5.2.
[39] Then the Adhvaryu himself [offers] with the portion for Ka.
He proceeds with a cake on one potsherd for Ka;
having proceeded with the cake on one potsherd for Ka, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Thereupon, the Adhvaryu cuts off a single portion from each of all the oblations, and then the Pratiprasthātṛ [cuts] from this very curd-mixture.
He cuts once; then, as he twice pours clarified butter over [the portions], they both step across.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite the offering prayer for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, they both make the offering.
Then the Adhvaryu alone cuts off the *prāśitra* (portion for consumption).
Having taken a portion from the *iḍā*, he hands it over to the Pratiprasthātṛ;

there also, the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off twice from the curd-mixture for the Maruts, then pours clarified butter over it twice from above, and having invoked the blessing, they purify themselves. 2.5.2 [41]
Then the Adhvaryu himself says, "O Brahman, I shall proceed;
O Agnīdh, having placed a kindling-stick, cleanse the fire.
Thereupon, the Adhvaryu pours out the clotted butter (pṛṣadājya) from the two offering-spoons; then, if there is clotted butter belonging to the Pratiprasthātṛ—
He divides that [clarified butter] into two parts; moreover, there is no speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) there.
He divides that clarified butter which is in the *upabhṛt* ladle into two parts. Both of them step across [the altar];
having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Sacrifice to the gods," and "Sacrifice, sacrifice" at every fourth *anuyāja*.

They proceed with nine after-offerings while bringing together [the butter]. Thus, that there are nine fore-offerings and nine after-offerings, it is on both sides that he thereby releases creatures from the noose of Varuna—from here upwards and from there downwards. Therefore, there are nine fore-offerings and nine after-offerings. 2.5.2. [42]
Having set down both [the spoons], they separate the *sruks*;

having separated the *sruks* and anointed the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), and having reached toward the enclosing-stick and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says: "The divine Hotṛs are impelled for the utterance of auspicious speech; you are sent forth."

"O man, for the sake of the Sūktavāka"—with these words the Hotṛ begins the Sūktavāka; then both of them together pluck up the two Prastara-bunches, both throw them after [the fire], and both, having grasped blades of grass, sit waiting until the Hotṛ recites the Sūktavāka. 2.5.2. [43]
Then the Āgnīdhra says, "Throw [the wooden sword] into the fire.
Both of them throw it into the fire, and both touch themselves.
Then he says, "Call for the *saṃvāda* (call-and-response)."
"Has the Āgnīdhra come? Make it heard! Śrauṣaṭ! A good journey to the divine Hotṛs;
well-being to the human ones; pronounce auspiciousness and prosperity!"—this is what the Adhvaryu says.
Then both of them throw the enclosing sticks (paridhis) into the fire together, and both, having taken up the offering-ladles (srucaḥ), set them down on the wooden sword (sphya). 2.5.2. [45]

Then the Adhvaryu, having returned, performs the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives; the Pratiprasthātṛ remains waiting. Having performed the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives, the Adhvaryu comes out. 2.5.2 [46]
He offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations.
The Pratiprasthātṛ silently takes up the offering-spoon.
Now, those two garments which were worn by the two sacrificers during the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should be used here as well; then, for this [offering] to Varuṇa...
Taking curds mixed with the scrapings from the parched grain, they go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). This is indeed related to Varuṇa; it is for the sake of release from Varuṇa.
No *sāman* is sung there, for nothing whatsoever is done with a *sāman* at that point; rather, having descended silently, he immerses himself. 2.5.2 [47]

"O Avabhṛtha, O Nicumpuṇa! You are the one who descends, O Nicumpuṇa. Through the gods, I have removed the sin committed against the gods; through mortals, I have removed the sin committed against mortals. O God, protect me from harm in the loud-voiced [battle]!"—for he may indeed fulfill the desire for whomever he may wish.

One should give [the garment] to him, for there are no two garments for one who has been initiated; just as a snake would be freed from its skin, so he is freed from all evil. 2.5.2. [48] Then, having shaved his hair and beard...

Having mounted the fires, he indeed performs this sacrifice as if after a formal departure (udavasāna), for it is not appropriate that one should offer the Agnihotra on the high altar (uttaravedi); therefore, he departs. Having gone to his home and churned out the fires, he sacrifices with the Full-moon offering (paurṇamāsa). For these Cāturmāsya sacrifices are, as it were, a ruined sacrifice; this [Full-moon sacrifice], however, is well-established.
The sacrifice is established when it is the full moon; thus, by means of this sacrifice properly arranged, he finally establishes himself.
Therefore, he concludes the rite. Prajāpati [performed] with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings.

He released the creatures from Varuna’s noose; thus his offspring were born free from disease and free from sin. Now, by means of these Sākamedha offerings, the gods slew Vṛtra and by means of them they indeed conquered;
that which was their victory, even so does this sacrificer, by means of these, [conquer] evil, the hating enemy, and the rival.
In that very way he slays and conquers; therefore, indeed, he sacrifices with these [offerings] in the fourth month. He sacrifices for two consecutive days. On the previous day—

He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat. For the gods, having made Agni their vanguard, went forth intending to slay Vṛtra; that Agni, being brilliance, did not waver. In the same way, this sacrificer, intending to slay his evil, hateful rival, goes forth having made Agni his very vanguard; he [is] brilliance.
Fire does not waver; therefore, [he offers] to Agni Anīkavat.
Then, at midday, he prepares a *caru* for the Maruts Sāṃtapanas. For indeed, the Maruts...
The Sāṃtapana Maruts scorched Vṛtra at midday; scorched, he lay there split open, breathing as if without food.
In the same way, the Sāṃtapana Maruts scorch the evil, the hating rival of this sacrificer; therefore [the offering is made] to the Sāṃtapana Maruts. 2.5.3. [4]
Then, for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins,
having driven away the calves with a branch and having milked [the cows] into a vessel containing a strainer,
he cooks that *caru*; for it is indeed a *caru* wherever they pour in the rice-grains— that is the sacrificial essence (*medhas*) for the gods.

In the morning they took up the water, intending to slay Vṛtra; and in the same way, this sacrificer, intending to slay his evil, hateful rival, takes up the cloud. As for why there is rice cooked in milk: milk is indeed the cloud, and rice grains are the cloud;
he thus places both kinds of cloud within himself. That is why there is rice cooked in milk. 2.5.3. [5]
Its covering is the very same [grass] that was spread for the Maruts Sāṃtapanas; upon that very spread-out altar, they place the enclosing sticks and the wood chips.
Having thus caused the milk to be collected, he cooks the *caru*;
having cooked it, he bastes it with clarified butter and removes it from the fire. 2.5.3. [6]
Then he washes two small plates or two bowls;
they divide the rice between those two, and having made a hollow for pouring ghee in the middle of them, he pours ghee into them. He cleans the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles, and then these—

Having taken up the rice-offering, he comes forward; and having taken up both the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladle (*sruk*), he comes forward. Having touched this very altar which has been strewn with grass, and having laid the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) around, he places as many wood-shavings as he desires upon the fire. Then he sets down these portions of rice, and he sets down both the dipping-spoon and the offering-ladle. The Hotṛ priest sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat, and [he places] the dipping-spoon.
Taking up the *sruva* ladle, he says:
"Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni.
He [offers] the portion of clarified butter belonging to Agni from the southern rice-pot.

Having poured ghee and having taken four portions of clarified butter, he steps across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Soma."

He takes four portions of clarified butter from the ghee-pouring over the northern rice-oblation for the gentle portion of clarified butter; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Soma," and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 2.5.3. [9]
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts, the householders.
He spreads a base of clarified butter from that portion of the southern rice-mess where the clarified butter is poured; of that—

He cuts twice; then he pours clarified butter over it from above, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins! At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he makes the offering.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."
From that clarified butter poured over the northern boiled rice, he makes an under-layer of ghee;
from that he takes two portions, then pours ghee over the top, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he addresses Agni.

"Recite the offering prayer for Sviṣṭakṛt"; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation. Then he cuts off the *iḍā* portion; there is no *prāśitra*. Having invoked the blessing, they perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*). This is one way of proceeding. 2.5.3. [11] Now, this is the second way.
That very [altar] which has been strewn for the Maruts Sāṃtapanas becomes the sacrificial altar;

upon that very strewn altar they place the enclosing sticks and the wood chips. Having thus caused the milk to be collected, he cooks the *caru*; he does not, however, place the clarified butter on the fire in the same manner as the neighbor’s [usual practice].

Having cooked [the oblation], having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having removed it from the fire, he anoints it; he removes the clarified butter into the pot and cleanses both the *sruva* and the *sruk* spoons. Then, taking that very *caru* together with its vessel, he goes out; taking the clarified butter from the pot, he goes out; and taking both the *sruva* and the *sruk*, he goes out. He [spreads] this very [barhis-grass]...

Having touched the altar and laid the enclosing sticks around it, he places as many wood-shavings as he desires upon the fire; then he sets down that very *caru* in its pan, places the clarified butter in the pot, and sets down the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles.
The Hotṛ sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat, and taking up the *sruva* and the *sruk*, he says: 2.5.3.[12]
"Recite for Agni!

Having taken four portions of clarified butter from the pot for the *ājyabhāga* belonging to Agni, he steps across; having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and [the offering is made] at the *vaṣaṭ* call.
He offers the oblation (juhoti). Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Soma";
he [offers] the portion of clarified butter belonging to Soma from the very vessel.

Having taken four portions of clarified butter, he steps across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Soma," and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Maruts, the householders.
He spreads a layer of clarified butter, and then—

He cuts off two portions from the meat, then pours clarified butter over them from above, anoints the places from which the portions were cut, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins. At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he makes the oblation.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."

He spreads clarified butter [as an under-layer] and then takes a single portion from this sacrificial pap; then he pours clarified butter over it twice. He does not re-anoint the portion that was cut off. Having stepped across, and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."
He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered (2.5.3).
Then he cuts off only the *iḍā*, not the *prāśitra*.
Having invited [the guests], those members of the household who are entitled to eat the remnants of the sacrificial food partake of it.

As many as there may be, they should eat; then the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should eat, and then other Brahmins should eat, if there should be much rice. Then, having covered this pot (*kumbhī*) which has not been emptied, they set it aside for the sake of the "full-spoon" offering. They let the calves join their mothers; thereby the cattle take the sacrificial food (*medha*) into themselves.
On that night he offers the Agnihotra with barley-gruel; they milk the cow to be slaughtered for the Pitṛyajña in the morning.
Then, whether the morning offering has been made or not, whichever way he may desire, from that undrunk pot of hers—

He strikes with the ladle: "Full, O ladle, fly away; full, fly back again! Like two bargaining merchants, O Śatakratu, let us exchange food and strength. Just as there is a *puro'nuvākya* verse, so too does he, by means of this [verse], summon him for this portion. 2.5.3. [18]
Then he should say, "Let us call the bull.
If it should bellow, some say that this is the *vaṣaṭ*-call;
at that *vaṣaṭ*-call he should offer the oblation. Moreover, he thereby calls Indra by his own form for the sake of Vṛtra.
For this bull is indeed the form of Indra; he thus calls him by his own form for the slaying of Vṛtra.

If it should bellow, he should know: "Indra has come to my sacrifice; my sacrifice is accompanied by Indra. But if it should not bellow, the Brāhmaṇa sitting to the south should say, "Offer! For that is the speech of Indra. 2.5.3. [19]
He offers [the oblation], saying: "Give to me; I give to thee. Bestow upon me; I bestow upon thee. Thou bringest a gift to me; may I bring a gift to thee. Svāhā!
Then [he offers] to the sportive Maruts.

He offers a cake on seven potsherds; for the sporting Maruts indeed approached Indra when he was about to slay Vṛtra and sported around him, magnifying him. In the same way, they sport around this one who is about to slay his evil, hateful rival.

Therefore, they magnify [the sacrifice] for the Maruts, the playful ones; and now, regarding the Mahāhavis itself—just as it is with the Mahāhavis, so it is with this [sacrifice]. Indeed, by means of the Mahāhavis, the gods slew Vṛtra.
By means of that very [sacrifice], they conquered; whatever victory was theirs, that they won.
In the same way, this [sacrificer] now slays evil, the hateful rival, by means of this [sacrifice], and in the same way he conquers.
Therefore, indeed, he performs this sacrifice. 2.5.4. [2]

Its ritual procedure is as follows: they strew the *uttaravedi*, they take the *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter), they churn the fire, there are nine *prayājas* and nine *anuyājas*, there are three *samiṣṭayajus* offerings; then there are these same five oblations. 2.5.4. [3]
As for the fact that there is a cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni:
it was indeed by means of Agni’s brilliance that they struck him down;
yet Agni, the brilliance, did not waver. Therefore, it is dedicated to Agni. 2.5.4 [4]
Now, as for the fact that there is a rice-oblation for Soma:
they slew him with King Soma; therefore, he has Soma as his king, and for that reason there is a rice-oblation for Soma. 2.5.4 [5]
Now, as for the cake for Savitṛ: it is either on twelve potsherds or on eight potsherds. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods;
impelled by Savitṛ, they slew him. Therefore, there is this offering to Savitṛ. 2.5.4. [6]
Now, as for the fact that there is a *sārasvata* oblation of cooked rice:
Sarasvatī is indeed Speech; it was Speech itself that cheered him on, saying, "Strike! Slay!
Therefore, there is a *sārasvata* oblation of cooked rice. 2.5.4 [7]
Now, as for the fact that there is a pap for Pūṣan:
this earth, indeed, is Pūṣan; she delivered him over to his slayer, and by her he was delivered over and they slew him. That is why there is a pap for Pūṣan. 2.5.4 [8]
Then there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni;
by this very means they slew him. Agni is brilliance and Indra is power and vigor; with these two powers they slew him. Or rather, it is the Brahman.

Agni and Indra are the two powers; having grasped both the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*), and having made them joined together, they slew him by means of those two heroic powers. Therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni. 2.5.4. [9]
Now there is an oblation of cooked rice for Mahendra.
Indeed, he was Indra before the slaying of Vṛtra;
but having slain Vṛtra, he became Mahendra, just as a great king becomes [Mahārāja] after conquering. Therefore, there is an oblation of cooked rice for Mahendra.
He indeed makes him great for the slaying of Vṛtra; therefore, there is also a pap for Mahendra.
Then there is a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman.

This entire rite was performed and everything was conquered by the gods when they had sacrificed with the Sākamedha offerings and were victorious; indeed, this entire rite is performed and everything is conquered by him who has sacrificed with the Sākamedha offerings and is victorious. Therefore, it belongs to Viśvakarman.

There is a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla-puroḍāśa). By means of this sacrifice, indeed, the gods, having sacrificed, became that which is this progeny of the gods and that which is their glory; and so, indeed, [does he become].
He who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice with this offering, procreates offspring and attains this prosperity; therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice. 2.6.1.1.
By means of the Mahāhavis, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra.
By means of that very [sacrifice], they conquered; whatever victory was theirs, that they won. And those whom they had slain in that battle, they restored by means of the Pitṛyajña.
They were indeed the Pitṛs (Fathers); therefore it is called the Pitṛyajña. 2.6.1. [2]
Spring, summer, and the rainy season—these are those which they conquered; autumn, winter, and the cool season—those are the ones which they restored again. 2.6.1 [3]
Now, as to why he sacrifices with this [offering]:

it was indeed because the gods performed it thinking, "In that way, they shall not kill anyone at all," that he now performs it; and whatever portion the gods assigned to them, that very portion he provides for them.
He thus makes this share for them; he protects both those gods whom [the others] have caused to fall away and their own [allies];

and he leads his own ancestors to a higher world. Furthermore, whatever of his own self is here destroyed or diminished by his lack of action, that is restored for him by this [rite]. Therefore, indeed, he performs this sacrifice. 2.6.1 [4]

He offers a cake on six potsherds to the Soma-possessing fathers, or to Soma accompanied by the fathers; for there are six seasons, and the fathers are the seasons; therefore it consists of six potsherds. 2.6.1. [5]
Then, for the *barhiṣat* ancestors, they prepare roasted grains (*dhānā*) on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire;
then they grind half of them, while the other half remains unground—thus the roasted grains become "un-ground" (*apiṣṭā*). These roasted grains are for the *barhiṣat* ancestors. 2.6.1. [6]
Then, for the Agniṣvātta ancestors, there is a stirred drink (mantha) made from the milk of a cow that has recently calved, churned once with a single stirring-stick;
for the ancestors have departed once and for all, therefore it is stirred only once. These [are the offerings].
The oblations are as follows: 2.6.1.
[7] Now, those who have sacrificed with Soma are the Pitṛs associated with Soma; and those who conquer the world by means of what is given and cooked are the others.

The Pitṛs who sit on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad); then those who are neither of these two, whom Agni himself consumes and makes savory—those Pitṛs are the Agniṣvātta-s. These are the Pitṛs. 2.6.1.
[8] He [places the fire] behind the Gārhapatya.

Having placed the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and sitting facing south, he takes this cake on six potsherds; rising from that very spot, standing to the north of the Anvāhāryapacana fire and facing south, he threshes the grain; he cleans it once, for they indeed go away once.
Therefore, he threshes once for the ancestors.
He places the lower and upper grinding stones only on the south side,
in the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire-chamber.
He lays down six enclosing-stones. As to why they attend upon this southern quarter—it is because this quarter belongs to the Fathers;
therefore they attend upon this southern quarter.
Then, to the south of the Anvāhāryapacana fire...
He makes the altar four-cornered; he makes the corners along the intermediate directions.
There are indeed four intermediate directions, and the ancestors are the intermediate directions; therefore, he makes the corners along the intermediate directions.

In the midst of that, he establishes the fire. For the gods turned westward from the east toward men; therefore, one offers to them while standing facing the east. The ancestors are on all sides, including the intermediate directions.
For the ancestors are indeed on all sides, as are these intermediate directions; therefore, he establishes the fire in the middle.
He then carries away the *stambayajus* from that very spot toward the east;
having offered the *stambayajus*, he proceeds thus at the outset.
He encloses it, saying "Now, now," and having enclosed it with the preceding enclosure, he writes or carries away whatever is to be carried;

he likewise encloses it with the subsequent enclosure, and having enclosed it with the subsequent enclosure and smoothed it down, he says, "Place the sprinkling waters! and they place the sprinkling waters; they set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass.

He cleanses the *sruva* and *sruca* ladles; having risen with the clarified butter (*ājya*), he becomes one wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) and takes portions of the clarified butter.

Regarding this, they say: "One should take two portions in the *upabhṛt* ladle, for there are two after-offerings (*anuyāja*) here. However, one should take eight times in the *upabhṛt*, lest one should depart from the established order of the sacrifice. Therefore, one takes eight times in the *upabhṛt*.
Having taken the clarified butter, he should take it up; then, having again placed the sacred thread over his right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), the Adhvaryu takes the sprinkling waters.
He first sprinkles the fuel-wood, then the altar, and then the sacrificial grass for him.

They give it; he places it before him with a knot. Having sprinkled it and poured water over it, he unties the knot but does not take up the *prastara* grass-bundle, for the ancestors have indeed departed once and for all; therefore, he does not take up the *prastara*. Then, having loosened the binding cord along [the bundle], he sets it down.
Moving counter-clockwise, he goes around three times while spreading the grass;
having thus spread it three times counter-clockwise, he leaves a remnant as far as the place for the *prastara* bundle.
Then he again goes around three times clockwise; in that he again goes around three times clockwise, he [offers] to those very same three ancestors whom he has followed.
Thus this [fire] moves away again toward this world of his; therefore he goes around it three times from left to right. He lays down the enclosing-sticks (paridhis) only on the south side;
he spreads the grass-bunch (prastara) on the south side, and does not place the two separating-blades (vidhṛtī) between them.
For the ancestors have departed once and for all; therefore, he does not place a separating barrier between them. 2.6.1 [17] There he places the *juhū* ladle;
then the *upabhṛt* to the east; then the *dhruvā*; then the sacrificial cake.
Having placed the parched grains (*dhānā*) and then the stirred drink (*mantha*) [on the altar], he touches the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
2.6.1.[18] Then all of them, having become invested with the sacred thread (*yajñopavītinaḥ*), proceed: thus the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the Brahman priest (*brahmā*), having gone around behind.
The Agnīdh stands in front.
With that [cup], they proceed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Indeed, the ancestors are as if hidden; this [low-voiced proceeding] is as if hidden. Therefore, they proceed in a low voice.
They move about in an enclosed space.
The ancestors, indeed, are as if hidden; and that which is enclosed is, as it were, hidden. Therefore they move about in an enclosed space.
2.6.1 [21] Now, while placing the fuel on the fire, he says:

"Recite for Agni as he is being kindled! Thus the Hotṛ recites only one *sāmidhenī* verse three times; for the fathers have departed once and for all, therefore the Hotṛ recites one *sāmidhenī* verse three times. 2.6.1 [22]
He recites: "Desiring thee, we set thee down; desiring, may we kindle thee.
Desiring, bring hither the desiring fathers to eat the oblation. Then he says: "Bring Agni; bring Soma;
bring the Soma-drinking fathers; bring the Barhis-sitting fathers; bring the Agni-consumed fathers; bring the gods who drink the clarified butter; bring Agni..."

"Bring [the gods] for the office of the Hotṛ; bring your own majesty! Having thus invoked them, he sits down. (2.6.1) Then, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he does not choose a Hotṛ, thinking: "This is a sacrifice to the ancestors; let me not place a Hotṛ among the ancestors."

Therefore, he does not choose a *hotṛ*; he simply says, "Sit down, O *hotṛ*! and the *hotṛ* sits down on the *hotṛ*-seat. Having sat down, he gives the impulse (*prasauti*). Being impelled, the *adhvaryu*, taking up the two offering-spoons, steps across toward the west. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the *samidhs*. He performs four fore-offerings (*prayāja*s) excluding the *barhis*. For the *barhis* is offspring; let him not [place] offspring among the fathers.

Thinking, "I shall support [the world]," he therefore performs four fore-offerings (prayāja) excluding the one for the sacrificial grass (apabarhiṣaḥ). Then they proceed with the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga).
Having proceeded with the two butter-portions, they all, having become invested with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ), [perform the next rites].

When they are about to proceed with these oblations, the sacrificer and the Brahman walk around in front, while the Āgnīdhra walks behind; then they cause the announcement to be made: "Oṃ svadhā! The response is "Astu svadhā," and the *vaṣaṭ*-call is "svadhā namaḥ. 2.6.1 [25]
Regarding this, Āsuri said:

"They should indeed cause the announcement to be made, they should respond to the announcement, and they should utter the *vaṣaṭ* call; let us not deviate from the established procedure of the sacrifice.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Soma-possessing Fathers," or "for Soma accompanied by the Fathers. He recites two invitatory verses;
for with one they cause the gods to move forward, and with two the Fathers, since they have indeed once for all departed.
Therefore, he recites two invitatory verses (puro’nuvākyā) for the Pitṛs.
He spreads a layer of clarified butter (ājya).
Then he cuts portions from this sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); he cuts them together with that [butter], and likewise together with the parched grains (dhānā).

He places that [portion] from the stirred offering once; then he sprinkles it twice with clarified butter from above, anoints the portions [from which they were cut], and does not step across [the altar]. Having risen from right there and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the Soma-possessing Fathers!
and offers when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 2.6.1. [28]
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Barhiṣad Pitṛs.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter [in the ladle], then cuts off portions of these parched grains; he cuts off a portion of the stirred drink together with that, and a portion of the cake together with that.
He places that [portion] once; then he pours clarified butter over it twice from above, bastes the cut-off portions, and does not step across [the altar].

Rising from his very place, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*). At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Pitṛs consumed by Agni (*agniṣvātta*)."

He spreads clarified butter [as a base], and then he cuts off a portion from this stirred drink; he places it together with that very same [portion] of the cake, and together with that, the parched grains.
He deposits all of that at once, and then he pours clarified butter over it twice from above and anoints the portions that have been cut off.
Without stepping across [the space], he rises and, having caused [the announcement] to be heard, says, "Sacrifice to the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Then he says, "Recite for Agni Kavyavāhana.
That [offering] is for Sviṣṭakṛt; for Kavyavāhana is indeed the bearer of oblations for the gods.
Kavyavāhana is the carrier of offerings for the ancestors; therefore, one says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Kavyavāhana.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter [on the ladle], and then he cuts portions from this sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); he cuts them together with that very [butter], and likewise together with the parched grains (dhānāḥ).
He places that [portion] from the stirred mixture once; then he pours clarified butter over it twice from above.

He does not anoint the portions back, nor does he step across. Rising from right there, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni Kavyavāhana," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 2.6.1. [32]
As for the fact that he does not step across:
rising from this very spot, he offers the oblation, for the fathers have indeed once and for all departed;
and as for the fact that he takes portions from all [the dishes] at once, it is because the fathers have indeed once and for all departed.
In that he cuts the portions crosswise, the ancestors are indeed the seasons;
thus he interlinks the seasons and joins the seasons together. Therefore, he cuts the portions crosswise.
Now, some place this very mash for the Hotṛ; the Hotṛ, having invited him, merely smells it. That...

He hands it to the Brahman; the Brahman indeed smells it. He hands it to the Āgnīdhra; the Āgnīdhra indeed smells it. They do this very thing; however, just as they cut off portions of the *iḍā* and the *prāśitra* for another sacrifice, so too should they cut off portions for this one. Having invoked it, they smell it but do not eat it.
"We think it should indeed be tasted," so said Āsuri, "of whatever [oblation] one offers into the fire.
Now, whichever of the two is about to give—
whether the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer— he takes a vessel of water and, moving counter-clockwise...

Sprinkling water three times, he goes around [the fire]. He causes the sacrificer’s father to wash his hands, saying, "O so-and-so, wash! "O so-and-so, wash! for the grandfather; "O so-and-so, wash! for the great-grandfather. Just as one would pour water over someone who is being consecrated, so it is in this case. 2.6.1. [35]

Then, having taken a portion of this sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), he places it in his left hand; having taken a portion of the parched grains (dhānā), he places them in his left hand; having taken a portion of the stirred drink (mantha), he places it in his left hand. 2.6.1[36]
He gives to the father of the sacrificer on that corner which extends toward this intermediate direction, saying,
"O so-and-so, this for you"; then he gives to the grandfather of the sacrificer on that corner which extends toward this intermediate direction.

He gives [the portion], saying, "This one, this much, for such-and-such. Then, on that corner which runs along this intermediate direction, he gives to the great-grandfather of the sacrificer, saying, "This one, this much, for such-and-such.
Then, on that corner which runs along this intermediate direction, he wipes [the vessel], saying, "O Fathers, rejoice here; partake according to your respective portions!"
"Partake according to your respective portions"—this is what he says by this. Thus, when he gives to the ancestors in this manner, he does not exclude his own ancestors from this sacrifice.
Then they all, having become invested with the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavītin*), [proceed].
Having gone out toward the north, they stand worshipping the Āhavanīya fire.
He who has established the sacred fires and performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices approaches the gods;
yet, because they have just performed the Pitṛyajña, they now make amends to the gods. 2.6.1. [38]

With two verses addressed to Indra, they worship the Āhavanīya fire, for the Āhavanīya is indeed Indra: "They have eaten and rejoiced; the dear ones have shaken themselves free. The self-luminous sages have praised you with their newest hymn. Now, O Indra, harness your two bay steeds!
O Maghavan, we would honor you who are so fair to behold. Now, O you whose chariot-seat is full, being praised, you go forth."
"Yoke now, O Indra, thy two bay steeds to the barren cow. (2.6.1.39) Then, having returned, they stand worshipping the Gārhapatya fire with the verse:
"We now call hither the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa hymn."

"By the hymn of the fathers and by our prayers, may the mind come back to us for wisdom, for skill, for life, and that we may long behold the sun. May the divine folk grant us back our mind, O fathers, so that we may be united with the company of the living.
For they have indeed moved along as if by the sacrifice to the fathers; now they truly reach back toward the living. Therefore he says, "the living."
"May we attend the host," [he says].
(2.6.1.40) Now, whichever of the two gives [the gift], he, having again become *prācīnāvītī* and having approached, mutters: "They have rejoiced."

"May the fathers satisfy themselves according to their respective portions"—by this he means, "they have satisfied themselves according to their respective portions. 2.6.1 [41] Then, taking a vessel of water, he goes around three times sprinkling from left to right; this is for the sacrificer.

He washes the hand of the father, saying, "O so-and-so, wash yourself! "O so-and-so, wash yourself! for the grandfather; and "O so-and-so, wash yourself! for the great-grandfather. This is just as one would sprinkle water upon someone who has eaten.
Furthermore, when he goes around three times from left to right, sprinkling water, it is so that this rite may be completed by him in a clockwise direction.
Thus, he goes around it three times from left to right, sprinkling water again. Then, having lifted up the fringe of his garment, he pays homage;
for the fringe is sacred to the ancestors, therefore he lifts up the fringe.

He pays homage; "homage" (namas) is indeed sacrifice, so he thereby makes these [ancestors] worthy of sacrifice. He pays homage six times; for there are six seasons, and the ancestors are the seasons;

thus he establishes the sacrifice within the seasons. That is why he pays homage six times. [He says: "O ancestors, grant us houses! For the ancestors are the masters of houses; this is the prayer for blessing at this rite. 2.6.1 [43]
Having all put on their sacrificial threads (*yajñopavītin*),
intending to proceed with the two after-offerings (*anuyāja*), the sacrificer and the Brahman sit behind [the altar], while the Āgnīdhra sits in front and the Hotṛ sits on the Hotṛ’s seat. 2.6.1.[44]

Then he says, "O Brahman, I shall set forth. Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fires," and taking up the two offering-spoons, he steps across toward the west. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the gods! He performs two after-offerings (*anuyāja*), omitting the *barhis* (grass).

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is indeed offspring; [he does this] thinking, "Lest I place the offspring among the ancestors. Therefore, he performs two after-offerings (*anuyāja*) without sacrificial grass.
Then, having set down the two offering-spoons (*sruk*), he separates them;
having separated the two spoons, he anoints the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).

Having stepped onto the enclosing-sticks and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, [the Adhvaryu says]: "The divine Hotṛs have been impelled; the human one has been sent forth for the recitation of the *sūktavāka*.
Thereupon, the Hotṛ begins the *sūktavāka*. The Adhvaryu does not pluck the *prastara* bundle; he simply remains waiting. When the Hotṛ recites the *sūktavāka*, [the Adhvaryu acts]. 2.6.1. [46]
Then the Āgnīdhra says, "Throw [the wooden sword] into the fire!
He does not throw anything into it at all; he merely touches himself while remaining silent.
Then he says, "Call for the *saṃvāda* (response)."
"O Āgnīdhra, go! Make it heard! "Śrauṣaṭ! "A good way for the divine Hotṛs;

well-being for the human ones; speak of peace and prosperity!"—with these words he merely touches the enclosing sticks (paridhis) but does not throw them into the fire; then he gathers this sacrificial grass (barhis) together with the enclosing sticks. 2.6.1 [48]

Now, some indeed collect the remains of the oblation together; but one should not do so. For these are the remains of what has been offered; [thinking], "Let us offer these remains of the offering into the fire," they should either throw them into water or eat them. By means of the Mahāhavis, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra.

By means of these very [offerings], they conquered that victory which was theirs; and those arrows which had struck them in that battle, they extracted as splinters by means of these very [offerings], and they pulled them out when they sacrificed with the Tryambaka offerings. 2.6.2. [2]
Now, as to why he sacrifices with these [oblations]:
"Surely no arrow of his ever misses its mark," so the gods thought; and it is for this very reason that he performs this rite.
Furthermore, both kinds of his offspring—those already born and those yet unborn—are thereby protected.
He releases them from Rudra; his offspring are born free from disease and free from blemish. For this reason, he performs sacrifice with these [oblations].
They indeed belong to Rudra.

For Rudra’s arrow is [single]; therefore they belong to Rudra. They consist of a single *kapāla* (potsherd), for they are intended to be dedicated to a single deity; therefore they consist of a single *kapāla*. These indeed correspond to each person.
As many domestic animals as there may be, they become one more than that;
by means of each one of these, he releases from Rudra's power those offspring of his that have already been born. They become one more than that;
by means of that one which is in excess, he releases from Rudra's power those offspring of his that are yet unborn. Therefore, they become one more than that. 2.6.2. [5]

Behind the Gārhapatya fire, having placed the sacrificial cord over his left shoulder (yajñopavītī) and sitting facing north, he takes these [grains]. Rising from that very spot and standing facing north, he threshes them; he places the lower and upper grinding stones in the northern half [of the altar].
He places the potsherds for the Gārhapatya fire. As to why they resort to that northern quarter—it is because this is the direction of this deity;
therefore they resort to that northern quarter.
They should indeed be smeared with butter.
"For the sacrificial oblation is already anointed; they should indeed remain unanointed. Rudra is prone to arrogance;
he might [harm] the cattle if one were to anoint them. Therefore, they should remain unanointed. Having placed them together in a single vessel, he sets them aside.
Taking a firebrand from the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he goes out toward the north and offers an oblation;
for this is the direction of that deity. He offers on the path, for that deity moves along the path. He offers at a crossroads, for a crossroads is indeed his well-known and familiar place of rest.
Therefore, he offers at a crossroads (2.6.2).
He offers with the middle leaf of a *palāśa* tree; for the leaf of the *palāśa* is indeed Brahman.
He offers this with a *brahman* formula. He cuts portions from all [the victims], but he does not cut a portion from that one which remains as a surplus.
He offers it with the words: "This is thy portion, O Rudra; together with thy sister Ambikā, enjoy it, Svāhā! For Ambikā indeed...
Nāma is his sister; with her he has this share, namely that which is his share together with a woman.
Therefore they are called Tryambakas. Whatever offspring of his is born, he releases them from Rudra’s power.
Now, as for that one who remains in excess—
"This heap of tobacco-dust, O Rudra, is your portion;
the rat is your animal"—thus he assigns the rat specifically among the animals for him, and thereby he does not harm the other animals.
Now, as to why he scatters [the dust]: embryos are indeed hidden away, and that which is scattered is hidden away; therefore, he scatters it.
"Thus he releases those of his offspring that are yet unborn from the power of Rudra. Then, having returned, they mutter:
"We have appeased Rudra, we have appeased the god Tryambaka, so that..."

"May he make us more submissive, may he make us better, may he cause us to exert ourselves; you are a remedy, a remedy for the cow, for the horse, a remedy for man, a remedy for the ram and the ewe"—this is the blessing of this rite. 2.6.2 [12]
Then they walk around three times counter-clockwise, striking their left thighs, [reciting]: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May he release me from death, as a cucumber from its stem."

"This is indeed a blessing of immortality for this rite; it is this very blessing that he invokes. For truly, only one who is released from death is as if at peace, not one who is not released from immortality.
Therefore he says: 'May I be released from death, may I not [be released] from immortality.
2.6.2. [13] And so, even children have gone around [this fire].
"Let us share in Bhaga's fortune. Now, she who is Rudra’s sister, named Ambikā, rules over Bhaga; therefore, even today, young maidens go about saying, "Let us share in Bhaga's fortune.
For them there is this mantra:
"We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the bestower of husbands;
may I be released from here like a cucumber from its stem—neither from here nor from there. When she says "from here," she means "from her kinsmen."
"May [the gods] not take me away"—this he says for the sake of the husbands, for the husband indeed is the support of a woman; therefore he says, "May they not take me away.
Then they walk around three times again in a sunwise direction, striking their right thighs with this same mantra.

Now, as for why they again circumambulate three times in a clockwise direction: it is so that this rite may be completed in a clockwise manner; therefore, they again circumambulate three times in a clockwise direction. Then the sacrificer, having poured these [grains] into his joined palms—
He throws it upwards so that the cow may not reach it;
thus they fashion these [embers] out of their own selves. Desiring to seize them, they touch them with water;
they thereby provide a remedy. Therefore, when desiring to seize them, they touch them with water. 2.6.2. [17]
Having tied those two bags together, having fastened them on both sides to a bamboo pole or to a post, he goes toward the east;
if he should find a tree, or a stump, or a bamboo, or an anthill, he hangs them upon it, saying: "This is for thee."
"O Rudra, go with the *avasa* beyond the Mūjavat mountains"—for people travel along a road with *avasa* (protection/sustenance); thus he directs him toward that very *avasa*.
Wherever his course lies, he follows it; and indeed, his course lies beyond the Mūjavats.
Therefore he says, "Go beyond the Mūjavats," [adding] "with bow unstrung, O wielder of the Pināka."
"Thus, 'being non-violent, O auspicious one, pass by us'—this is what he says. 'Clad in a skin'—he thereby puts him to sleep; for while sleeping, he does not harm anyone.
Therefore he says, 'clad in a skin. (2.6.2)
Then they turn toward their right arms;
looking back, they return again, and having returned, they touch water.

For they have indeed moved along with that which belongs to Rudra, and water is a means of pacification; thus they pacify themselves by means of that water, which is a means of pacification. 2.6.2 [19]

Then, having shaved his hair and beard and having consigned the fires into himself, he moves away from the sacrificial ground; for it is with this [rite] that he sacrifices, as it is not appropriate that he should offer the Agnihotra on the high altar (uttaravedi).
Therefore, he moves away; having gone to his own home, he churns out the fires.

He performs the Full-moon sacrifice. These Cāturmāsya sacrifices are, as it were, a neglected sacrifice; whereas the Full-moon sacrifice is a well-ordered and firmly established sacrifice. Thus, by means of that well-ordered sacrifice, he finally establishes himself. Therefore, he concludes [the Cāturmāsyas] with the Full-moon sacrifice. 2.6.3.1.
Truly, the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices becomes inexhaustible.
For he conquers the year; therefore, his merit becomes inexhaustible. Indeed, having divided that [sacrifice] threefold, he sacrifices; having divided it threefold, he conquers.

The year is indeed everything, and everything is imperishable; by this, his good deed becomes imperishable. Having become the season itself, he goes even unto the gods; for the gods are indeed imperishable, and by this, his good deed becomes imperishable. This, then, is why one sacrifices with the Cāturmāsya offerings. 2.6.3. [2]
Now, as to why one should sacrifice with the *Cunāsīrya*:

that which was the glory (*śrī*) of the gods when they had performed the *Sākamedha* sacrifices and were victorious—that was the *cuna*; and that which was the essence (*rasa*) of the year once it had been won—that was the *sīra*. And that which...

The prosperity of the gods who had sacrificed with the Sākamedha offerings and were victorious was this very thing; and whatever essence belonged to the year that had been completed—that same twofold [essence], having grasped it, he makes his own. Therefore, he sacrifices with the Cunāsīrya. 2.6.3. Its procedure is as follows: they do not prepare the high altar (uttaravedi), they do not take the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), and they do not churn the fire. Five...
There are three *prayāja* offerings, three *anuyāja* offerings, and one *samiṣṭayajus*. Now, these same five oblations are used;
indeed, by means of these oblations, Prajāpati [produced] offspring.

With these [offerings], he released creatures from the noose of Varuna on both sides; with these, indeed, the gods slew Vṛtra, and with these they conquered—that victory which was theirs. And so does this sacrificer, by means of these, attain both that prosperity which belonged to the gods when they had performed the Sākamedha sacrifices and were victorious, and that which belongs to the year that has been completed.
There was sap; having grasped both of these, he makes them his own. Therefore, there are these five oblations.
Then there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Śunāsīra.
That is the *bandhu* of the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice which we have previously stated.
Now, there is milk for Vāyu.

"Verily, milk is what creatures recognize when they are born, thinking, 'May the creatures recognize me, the victorious one, for the sake of prosperity, glory, and the eating of food. Therefore it is milk.
Now, as to why it belongs to Vāyu..."
This indeed is Vāyu, who blows here; he causes all this to swell, whatever it may be that rains here. When it has rained, plants are born;
having eaten the plants and drunk the water, from that milk comes into being from the waters. For he (Vāyu) indeed produces this; therefore it belongs to Vāyu.
2.6.3 [8] Now there is a sacrificial cake on one potsherd for Sūrya. He who shines yonder is indeed Sūrya;
he indeed protects all this, both by what is good and by what is not good. He ordains all this in accordance with what is good.
"May this [sacrifice] of yours not conquer me through what is unrighteous; may it protect me through what is righteous; may it grant me [the fruit] through what is righteous.
Because of this, there is a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla-puroḍāśa) dedicated to Sūrya.
Its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a white horse.

The form of that which shines yonder is thereby produced; if he should not find a white horse, even a white bull may be used, for its form is thereby produced as that which shines yonder. 2.6.3 [10] At whatever time he performs the Sākamedha sacrifices, [he does so].
One should sacrifice with the Taccunāsīrya; for in that he sacrifices three times in the year, by that very means he attains the year.
Therefore, one may sacrifice with this at any time whatsoever.
Regarding this, some desire to complete the nights. If he should desire to complete the nights, [he should do so] from that [time] prior to the month of Phālguna.
Having observed the full moon of Phālguna, one should sacrifice with the *Taittirīya* (or *Cunāsīrya*). Then he should undergo initiation;
the full moon of Phālguna should not pass him by while he has not yet sacrificed, for he would be like one who has set out on a journey again.

One should wait until the full moon of Phālguna; therefore, one should not wait until the full moon of Phālguna again for one who has not performed the sacrifice. On the day before the full moon of Phālguna, one should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrya; then in the morning, with the Vaiśvadeva; then with the Full-moon sacrifice. This is for one who performs [the rites] again. 2.6.3. Now, therefore, regarding the turning: yonder sun indeed faces every direction; he indeed sucks up all this world.
Insofar as whatever dries up is consumed by him, he is therefore the "consumer of food" (annāda) from every side.
This fire has faces on all sides;
for from whichever direction they place fuel into the fire, it burns from that very direction.
Therefore, he is "all-facing" (sarvatomukha), and for that reason, he is the "eater of food" (annāda).
Now, this person here has faces turned in one direction; he becomes all-facing when he turns himself around.
In this very way one becomes an eater of food, just as these two do; therefore, he who knows this should indeed cause them to revolve.
Regarding this, Āsuri said:
What indeed would be gained for the face even if one were to shave all the hair there?

Since he sacrifices three times a year, by that very act he becomes one whose face is turned in every direction and thus an eater of food; therefore, he need not concern himself with turning [the head]. 2.6.4.1.

Regarding what they say: "By the Sākamedha offerings, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra; by them they conquered that very victory which is theirs"—for it was indeed by all the Cāturmāsya sacrifices that the gods slew Vṛtra, and by all of them that they conquered.

"Whatever victory they have won," they said, "by what king and by what army shall we fight? Then Agni said, "By me as king, by me as army. With Agni as king and Agni as army, they conquered for four months; and with Brahman...

And they encompassed [the year] with the triple science (trayī vidyā). They said, "With whom as king, with whom as leader shall we fight? Varuṇa said, "With me as king, with me as leader. With Varuṇa as king and Varuṇa as leader, they [fought] for another four months.

They conquered them by means of the sacred word (*brahman*) and the threefold knowledge (*trayi-vidyā*), and they encompassed them. They said, "With what king and with what army shall we fight? Indra said, "With me as king and with me as the army. Thus, with Indra as their king and Indra as their army, [they fought] for another four months.
They conquered them by means of the *brahman* and the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), and they encompassed them. When he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva [offering],
it is as if he conquers the four months by means of Agni himself as king, with Agni as his vanguard.
That *śalalī* is three-spined and the razor is made of copper. That which is the three-spined *śalalī* is the form of the triple science (*trayī vidyā*);

the copper razor is the form of the Brahman. For Agni is the Brahman, and Agni is, as it were, red; therefore the razor is made of copper. With it he shaves. Thus he encloses him both with the Brahman and with the triple science. 2.6.4. [6]
Now, as to why he sacrifices with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings:

it is by means of Varuṇa himself, the king, and by means of Varuṇa as his vanguard, that he conquers the next four months. In this regard, there is a three-striped porcupine quill and a copper razor; with these he shaves [the hair], and that is by means of the Brahman.
And thus he encompasses him with this triple knowledge.
2.6.4. Now, when he sacrifices with the Sākamedha offerings, it is with Indra as king, with Indra as his vanguard, that he [conquers] the other four months.

He procreates that [offspring]. There is a three-striped porcupine quill and a copper razor; with these he shaves it around. Thus, by means of both the *brahman* and the triple knowledge (*trayi vidyā*), he encloses it. 2.6.4. [8] Now, as for why he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva [offering].
Then he becomes Agni himself; he wins union with Agni and residence in the same world as Agni.
Then, when he sacrifices with the Sākamedha offerings, he becomes Indra himself; he wins union with Indra and residence in the same world as Indra.
In whichever season he goes to that world, that season delivers him to the next season, and the next delivers him to the one beyond;
thus the performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices goes to the highest place and the supreme goal.
Regarding this they say: "They do not find fault with one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, for he indeed goes to the highest station and attains the supreme goal."
